messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
"A few, if you'll allow them," Sefa says, folding her hands over the prayer beads at her wrist. "How did Jassan Ferr die? If it was the fever, I'd want to know before we open his door — the room may still be... unpleasant. And is there anyone else with a key to that room, or a claim on his things? A landlord, a kinsman. I'd rather not walk into someone's grief or anger with my hands full."

She watches Vell's face as she asks, open and mild, the way she used to watch patients' families at the hospice when the truth was too much for them to say. After a moment she adds, "And the seal — is it your mark or his? I want to be sure we bring you the right box and not the wrong one."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell has been leaning on the end of the counter with his thumbs hooked in his belt, eyes drifting over the tidy clerk's desk — the capped inkwell, the clean blotter — and then back to Vell. He straightens up.

"A few things, since you're asking." He counts them off the way Vell did, one finger at a time. "One — who holds the key to Ferr's room now? The cooper, a landlady, you? If I'm to knock on a door I'd rather know whose door it is, and whether they've been told we're coming or whether they'll be sending for the Fist."

"Two — the box. How big, how heavy, what's the lock, and what does your seal look like? If someone's already been at it, I want to know what *whole* is meant to look like before I'm stood in the room guessing."

"Three — the man died three days ago. Has anyone been in since? Family, a friend, someone else who thinks they're owed? Anyone else asked you about those ledgers?" He keeps his voice easy, but his eyes are on Vell's hands when he asks it.

"And last — unopened I understand, you've said it twice. I'm only asking whether there's anyone in Beregost who'd rather it *stayed* in that room, so I know whether to walk there or go quiet."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I rest my shield’s rim against my boot.

“Three questions. What killed Ferr? Who’s had access to his room since? And who, if anyone, is likely to dispute your claim to that box?”

I glance at the unused desk, then back to Vell.

“We’ll need a note under your seal authorising the collection. Saves an argument with the landlord.”

cards.title: Insight: reading Vell's face as he answers who else wants the box

screens.Sefa Marrin:
Pell, leaning on the end of the counter, straightens and counts his questions off on his fingers. He asks who holds the key to Ferr's room and whether the holder knows you are coming, or might send for the Fist. He asks about the box: its size, its weight, its lock, and what Vell's seal looks like, so he knows what "whole" means. He asks whether anyone has been in the room in the three days since the death, and whether anyone else has asked about the ledgers. He finishes by asking whether anyone in Beregost would rather the box stayed where it is. While he asks, he keeps his voice easy and his eyes on Vell's hands.

Bram sets his shield's rim against his boot. He asks what killed Ferr, who has had access to the room since, and who might dispute Vell's claim to the box. He also asks for a note under Vell's seal authorising the collection, to save an argument with the landlord.

Vell hears all of you out without interrupting. He lifts one finger and answers in the order the questions came.

"His heart. The landlady found him in the morning, in his chair. No fever. The room is not unpleasant." He pauses. "It was not unpleasant when I last stood in it, at least. That was a month ago."

A second finger. "The key is with the landlady. Wenna Pike. She owns the rooms over the cooper's yard. Tobin the cooper has the yard and the shop below. Jassan had no kin in Beregost. His mother is dead, years ago, in the Gate. The temple took his body for burial. Since then, Wenna and whoever she lets in. I have not been."

He turns to Pell. "The box. Oak, bound in iron. This long." His hands set themselves on the counter about a foot and a half apart. "One man carries it. Heavy with paper, nothing else. A brass lock. The key is here, with me." He doesn't say where, and his hands don't move toward any drawer. "The seal is mine. Red wax across the lid seam, my mark. Scales, with a V beneath."

To Bram he gives a short nod and pulls a sheet of paper from under the counter. He writes quickly and plainly, in a moneylender's hand: *Wenna Pike: the bearers collect Jassan Ferr's strongbox on my behalf. O. Vell.* He warms a stick of red wax over the lamp, lets a drop fall at the foot of the page and presses a brass ring into it. When he lifts the ring the mark is just as he said: a small balance with a V beneath it, sharp in the red. He blows on it once and slides the note across to Bram.

Then he gets to Pell's last question, and to who else has asked. You watch his face. Pell watches his hands.

cards.title: Insight: reading Vell's face as he answers who else wants the box

presses.text:
Sefa holds Vell's gaze through the answer about the box's claimants — through the flat, practiced calm of a man who is used to being asked. She knows that look. At the hospice, people lied by keeping their faces and voices too still.

But Vell doesn't lie. When he says, "No one has asked me for the box," his voice stays even, and his eyes don't shift; and then, just for a breath, they do — not left or right, but at the clean, empty desk beside the counter. Jassan's desk. His knuckles whiten against the counter's edge, and then the hand opens and returns to rest.

When he looks back at you, the steadiness is there again, but with something sharper beneath it. Grief, you think. Or the kind of anger that comes when a lender loses a good clerk and won't waste it in front of hired people.

He says, dryly, "There is always someone in Beregost who would rather a strongbox stayed shut. That is what a strongbox is for." Then he settles his hands one over the other and waits to see if you have more for him.

His mother is dead, years ago, in the Gate. The temple took his body for burial. Since then, Wenna and whoever she lets in. I have not been."

He turns to Pell. "The box. Oak, bound in iron. This long." His hands set themselves on the counter about a foot and a half apart. "One man carries it. Heavy with paper, nothing else. A brass lock. The key is here, with me." He doesn't say where, and his hands don't move toward any drawer. "The seal is mine. Red wax across the lid seam, my mark. Scales, with a V beneath."

To Bram he gives a short nod and pulls a sheet of paper from under the counter. He writes quickly and plainly, in a moneylender's hand: *Wenna Pike: the bearers collect Jassan Ferr's strongbox on my behalf. O. Vell.* He warms a stick of red wax over the lamp, lets a drop fall at the foot of the page and presses a brass ring into it. When he lifts the ring the mark is just as he said: a small balance with a V beneath it, sharp in the red. He blows on it once and slides the note across to Bram.

Then he gets to Pell's last question, and to who else has asked. Sefa watches his face. Pell watches his hands.

"Has anyone asked." Vell squares the ink pot with the edge of the counter. "No one has come here asking for Jassan's ledgers." His hands are flat and still on the wood the whole time he says it. Pell sees a moneylender's hands, used to lying on a counter while a borrower begs, and they tell him nothing at all.

Sefa catches what the hands hide. *Come here asking* is a careful choice of words, and Vell says them like a man who has already checked that each one is true. The look on his face isn't grief for his clerk. It's closer to fear, and it isn't fear of the box. When he says *before nightfall* a second time, a moment later, his eyes go to the window and the street, not to the three of them. The hour matters to someone who isn't in this room.

"Who would rather it stayed put." He thinks about it honestly, or seems to. "Gerrit Thale keeps a counting-room at the south end of town, past the Jovial Juggler. He would like anything that is mine. He is a lender, not a cutpurse. Walk. You need not go quiet for Thale." He shuts the ledger in front of him. "Wenna Pike will want something from you. She always wants something. Jassan's debts were Jassan's."

He doesn't offer to pay them, and he doesn't look at the clerk's desk. Outside, on the Coast Way, a cart rattles past toward the smithies, and the hammers go on ringing through the shutters.

relay.request:
Characters at the table: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
In this scene: Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway.
Write the screens of, in this order: Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Sefa Marrin: "A few, if you'll allow them," Sefa says, folding her hands over the prayer beads at her wrist. "How did Jassan Ferr die? If it was the fever, I'd want to know before we open his door — the room may still be... unpleasant. And is there anyone else with a key to that room, or a claim on his things? A landlord, a kinsman. I'd rather not walk into someone's grief or anger with my hands full."

She watches Vell's face as she asks, open and mild, the way she used to watch patients' families at the hospice when the truth was too much for them to say. After a moment she adds, "And the seal — is it your mark or his? I want to be sure we bring you the right box and not the wrong one."

Pell Dunmore: Pell has been leaning on the end of the counter with his thumbs hooked in his belt, eyes drifting over the tidy clerk's desk — the capped inkwell, the clean blotter — and then back to Vell. He straightens up.

"A few things, since you're asking." He counts them off the way Vell did, one finger at a time. "One — who holds the key to Ferr's room now? The cooper, a landlady, you? If I'm to knock on a door I'd rather know whose door it is, and whether they've been told we're coming or whether they'll be sending for the Fist."

"Two — the box. How big, how heavy, what's the lock, and what does your seal look like? If someone's already been at it, I want to know what *whole* is meant to look like before I'm stood in the room guessing."

"Three — the man died three days ago. Has anyone been in since? Family, a friend, someone else who thinks they're owed? Anyone else asked you about those ledgers?" He keeps his voice easy, but his eyes are on Vell's hands when he asks it.

"And last — unopened I understand, you've said it twice. I'm only asking whether there's anyone in Beregost who'd rather it *stayed* in that room, so I know whether to walk there or go quiet."

Bram Halloway: I rest my shield’s rim against my boot.

“Three questions. What killed Ferr? Who’s had access to his room since? And who, if anyone, is likely to dispute your claim to that box?”

I glance at the unused desk, then back to Vell.

“We’ll need a note under your seal authorising the collection. Saves an argument with the landlord.”

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell's eyes stay on those hands a beat longer than is polite, then he gives it up with a small tilt of the head — a man who's looked at a locked door and decided it's a good lock.

"Fair enough." He pushes off the counter. "One last, and then we're your legs. Wenna Pike — what is it she'll want? If Ferr was behind on his rent, say so, and roughly by how much. I'd sooner know the number before she names it, than stand in her doorway while she decides what three strangers look like they're worth. And if it comes to it — does your note buy the box, or the box *and* whatever's in that room? Because a landlady with a dead tenant's goods and no kin to claim them has her own ideas about who's owed."

He glances at the tidy clerk's desk once more, then at Bram's note. "Keep that dry," he says to Bram, half a grin. "It's the only thing we're carrying that anyone has to respect."

Then, to Sefa and Bram both, moving toward the door: "I'd like to see the yard before we knock. Front, back, what's under his window. It costs us the time of a slow walk round the block, and I've never once regretted it."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I let the wax cool before folding the note clear of the seal and stowing it.

“If Wenna wants rent paid before she releases it, we’ll bring you her demand. We’ve agreed to carry a box, not settle Ferr’s debts.”

I turn to Sefa and Pell. “Ready? Best see what’s actually there.”

Unless either has more to ask, I head for the cooper’s yard with them, keeping my sword sheathed.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa presses her palms lightly on the edge of the counter, the beads clicking once against the wood. She says, "Before nightfall, then." Her voice is quiet and unhurried, the voice she used in the ward at the small hours, when a patient needed to believe the night would pass. "One more thing. If we arrive and the box has already been opened — if the seal is broken or the lid has been forced — what would you have us do? Bring it anyway, as we find it? Or leave it and come back for you first?"

She watches his face, not to trap him now, but to anchor him as she asks. Whatever Vell is afraid of, she thinks, he won't say it before strangers; but he may at least grant her an answer she can carry.

scenes.narration:
Vell takes Pell's question first, because it was asked first.

"She'll want rent. He was behind. I don't know by how much. A room over Tobin's yard doesn't cost much, and Jassan didn't spend much." He stops for a moment. "Ten days ago he asked me for his wage early. I said no. She may know that. She may not."

Then the second half. "The note covers the box. The box is mine, and the ledgers in it are mine. His bed, his coat, his debts are not mine, and I don't want them. If she says she's owed for them, she's owed by him and not by me. The temple has his body. She can settle with the temple."

Bram folds the note, keeping the fold clear of the wax, and puts it away. Vell watches the seal go out of sight and answers him with a short nod. "Bring me her number. I'll decide then."

Sefa's question comes last, quietly, and it lands harder than anything else anyone has asked this morning. Vell doesn't answer right away. His hands stay flat on the counter, but his mouth tightens at the corners. It's the face of a man doing a sum he already knows the answer to.

"Bring it," he says. "As you find it. Here, to me, and to nobody else on the way. Don't go anywhere first." Another pause. "If you know who opened it, bring me the name. The terms don't change. Unopened, seal whole, before nightfall. Anything else is not what I hired you for."

He looks down at the closed ledger in front of him, and the counting-house is quiet apart from the hammers.

Pell has the door open by then. The Coast Way is already busy outside: a smith's boy hauling a bucket of slack-water, a carter leaning on his reins, coal smoke drifting low across the cobbles. Bram follows him out onto the step, his sword sheathed and the note dry under his arm. A few hundred feet down the street, on the same side, stands the cooper's yard. Barrel staves are stacked in pale bundles against a board fence, there's a gate wide enough for a cart, and above the shop a row of shuttered windows sits under the eaves. One shutter is closed. The rest are open to the morning. Behind them, through the open door, Sefa is still at the counter with Vell's answer, and the moneylender has not lifted his eyes from his ledger.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I step aside from the doorway and wait for Sefa.

To Pell, quietly: “Have your look. I’ll speak to Wenna once Sefa joins us. If that seal’s already broken, we settle the price before carrying anything back. I don’t fancy doing the job and then arguing whether it counted.”

From the step, I look over the yard’s gate and upper windows, watching for anyone taking an interest in us.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the silence sit for one breath longer than is comfortable, then nods — once, slowly, as if accepting a charge rather than a bargain. "Bring it as we find it," she repeats. "To you, and only you. No stops." Her gaze touches Vell's bowed head, the closed ledger, the empty desk with its tidy, false stillness. "If we learn a name, you'll have it. You may not like the name."

She turns from the counter. At the threshold she pauses and looks back, her hand on the doorframe. "Vell," she says, not unkindly. "If someone comes for it before nightfall — someone who isn't us — send no one to warn us. We'll manage what's in the street." Then she is through the door, blinking in the morning glare, and she falls in with Bram and Pell on the Coast Way.

As they walk, she glances at the stacked barrel staves ahead, the open shutters and the one closed window above the cooper's shop. Her voice is low, for the two of them only. "I don't think he lied, but he omitted. The hour sits on him. Did either of you see it? He said *no one has come here asking* — not that no one wants it." The prayer beads click under her sleeve as she walks. "Tobin's yard. Let's see the street before we knock, as Pell said. And I want a look at that one closed shutter."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell steps down into the street and lets the traffic take him — not toward the cooper's gate but across the way, onto the opposite side, where a man can look at a row of windows without standing under them.

"Walk with me a minute, if you like, or wait for her," he says to Bram, low, with a nod back at the open door. "Either way, don't go in till we're all three at the gate. One shutter closed and the rest open — I'd put a silver on that being his, and I'd like to know who closed it. A dead man doesn't, and a landlady airing a room doesn't either."

He goes down the far side at an idle pace, eyes working: the closed shutter and what's under it — gutter, drainpipe, a stack of staves, a lean-to roof, anything a man could stand on; whether that window gives onto the street or the yard; which way the stairs to the rooms must run from where the door sits in the shop front. Then round the end of the board fence, if there's an alley or a lane, to see the back — a second door, a rear stair, a gap in the boards, and whether anyone's been through it lately.

He keeps his hands in plain sight and his hood down. A hireling looking for an address, nothing more.

"I wasn't going to send anyone," he says. Then the pen moves again, and that is all she gets from him.

Out on the step the morning is bright and loud. You stand to one side of the door with your shield rim against your boot and watch the street the way you used to watch a road before the wagons came up. You don't look for trouble. You look for whoever isn't busy.

Sefa comes out through the door, blinking in the glare, and falls in with you and Pell on the Coast Way. Pell has already stepped down into the street and gone across to the far side, where he can look over a row of windows without standing beneath them. He told you quietly to walk with him or wait for her, but not to go in until all three of you are at the gate. He said the one closed shutter among the open ones might well be the dead man's, and he wants to know who closed it. He then went on down that side at an idle pace, looking over the building and the board fence.

Sefa speaks low, for you and Pell only. She doesn't think Vell lied, but he left something out: he said no one had come asking, not that no one wanted it. She wants to see the street before knocking at Tobin's yard, and she wants a look at that closed shutter.

cards.title: Perception: watching the Coast Way for anyone taking an interest in the yard, or in the three of you

scenes.input:
(Round 3 — one paragraph per character in this scene. Close this scene on the world as it stands: no question, offer, demand or wait put to one character, and no out-of-game note — the table asks every player what they do next.)

Bram Halloway: I step aside from the doorway and wait for Sefa.

To Pell, quietly: “Have your look. I’ll speak to Wenna once Sefa joins us. If that seal’s already broken, we settle the price before carrying anything back. I don’t fancy doing the job and then arguing whether it counted.”

From the step, I look over the yard’s gate and upper windows, watching for anyone taking an interest in us.

Sefa Marrin: Sefa lets the silence sit for one breath longer than is comfortable, then nods — once, slowly, as if accepting a charge rather than a bargain. "Bring it as we find it," she repeats. "To you, and only you. No stops." Her gaze touches Vell's bowed head, the closed ledger, the empty desk with its tidy, false stillness. "If we learn a name, you'll have it. You may not like the name."

She turns from the counter. At the threshold she pauses and looks back, her hand on the doorframe. "Vell," she says, not unkindly. "If someone comes for it before nightfall — someone who isn't us — send no one to warn us. We'll manage what's in the street." Then she is through the door, blinking in the morning glare, and she falls in with Bram and Pell on the Coast Way.

As they walk, she glances at the stacked barrel staves ahead, the open shutters and the one closed window above the cooper's shop. Her voice is low, for the two of them only. "I don't think he lied, but he omitted. The hour sits on him. Did either of you see it? He said *no one has come here asking* — not that no one wants it." The prayer beads click under her sleeve as she walks. "Tobin's yard. Let's see the street before we knock, as Pell said. And I want a look at that one closed shutter."

Pell Dunmore: Pell steps down into the street and lets the traffic take him — not toward the cooper's gate but across the way, onto the opposite side, where a man can look at a row of windows without standing under them.

"Walk with me a minute, if you like, or wait for her," he says to Bram, low, with a nod back at the open door. "Either way, don't go in till we're all three at the gate. One shutter closed and the rest open — I'd put a silver on that being his, and I'd like to know who closed it. A dead man doesn't, and a landlady airing a room doesn't either."

He goes down the far side at an idle pace, eyes working: the closed shutter and what's under it — gutter, drainpipe, a stack of staves, a lean-to roof, anything a man could stand on; whether that window gives onto the street or the yard; which way the stairs to the rooms must run from where the door sits in the shop front. Then round the end of the board fence, if there's an alley or a lane, to see the back — a second door, a rear stair, a gap in the boards, and whether anyone's been through it lately.

He keeps his hands in plain sight and his hood down. A hireling looking for an address, nothing more.

scenes.narration:
Vell doesn't look up when Sefa speaks from the doorway. His pen stops over the ledger.

"I wasn't going to send anyone," he says. Then the pen moves again, and that is all she gets from him.

Out on the step the morning is bright and loud. Bram stands to one side of the door with his shield rim against his boot and watches the street the way he used to watch a road before the wagons came up. He doesn't look for trouble. He looks for whoever isn't busy.

The man is two doors up, on the same side as the counting-house, on a bench outside a pie-seller's hatch. He's young, broad in the shoulder, with a smith's forearms speckled with old burn scars. There's a mug of something beside him that he hasn't touched, and the steam went off it a while ago. When the counting-house door opened his head came up, and Bram watches him count: one, two, three. When Pell stepped off the step and crossed the street, the young man's head turned with him all the way over. Then his eyes went to the cooper's gate and stayed there. He has white on the fingertips of his right hand, chalk or flour, and he has wiped some of it down his trouser leg in a pale streak. A pie-seller's boy would have flour to the elbow. This one has it on three fingers. He isn't eating either.

Sefa comes out blinking into the glare and falls in at Bram's shoulder. She speaks low, for the two of them. Pell is already across the way and out of earshot, so her question reaches Bram and the street noise takes the rest. Tobin's mallet is going steadily somewhere in the yard, thock and thock, iron hoops going onto oak.

Across the Coast Way, Pell walks the far side at an address-hunter's pace and reads the building without needing to try. It's his trade, and the cooper's place isn't hard. The rooms above the shop all face the street, five windows under the eaves. The closed shutter is the end one, nearest the yard gate, and it's shut from the inside: no hasp or peg on the outer face. Below it, inside the board fence, a lean-to stave shed runs along the shop wall. Its shingled roof sits about ten feet off the ground and comes up to within seven feet of that sill. A man who climbs for a living could be at the shutter in the time it takes to say so. The shop door is on the left of the front. The way up to the rooms can't be inside the shop, so it must run up the yard side.

He goes round the end of the fence. A muddy lane runs behind it, with a midden heap and a cart rut. Over the fence he can see the stair, an outside wooden one climbing the side of the shop to a narrow gallery, with the rooms' doors opening off it. The back gate in the fence is barred from inside and hasn't been opened lately; the mud in front of it is smooth. The left-hand post of that gate has been marked, though, low at about knee height where a passer-by's eye never goes. It's a small chalk ring with a short stroke beneath it. Pell knows that hand from the Wide. It means *watched: someone's on this.* The chalk is fresh. The powder is still loose in the grain of the wood, and wind and damp haven't smeared it yet.

Back on the Coast Way, the young man on the bench picks up his cold mug at last, doesn't drink from it, and puts it down again. His eyes stay on the cooper's gate.

 Bram's watch pays off in full. Out of the whole busy morning on the Coast Way, he picks out the one man who has no business on it: the young smith on the pie-seller's bench, with the cold mug, the chalked fingers and his eyes on the cooper's gate. Bram has his face, his build and the pale streak on his trouser leg fixed in his mind. He has managed it without once looking straight at him, and the young man hasn't noticed he's been marked. It's the old road feeling coming back, the moment before the wagons crest a rise, when you already know where the trouble is sitting.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Bram ducks his head in a half-nod as he walks. "I saw the same," he says, low. "A moneylender with an empty desk and a shut eye." He glances toward the high board fence ahead. "Pell takes the back while we find the front. Stay close, both of you, until we know who's at home."

Pell is already drifting ahead, not hurrying, hands in his pockets like a man with no particular errand. As he passes the cooper's gate he turns his head once, scanning the boards, then slips into the shadow at the gate's near post and watches. Without the racket of the smithies, the yard sounds nearer now: the rasp of a drawknife on unseasoned wood, the thump of stacked staves, and somewhere a dog making a low, worried sound. The closed shutter sits above the shop like an eye gone shut while the others are still blinking in the light.

What does Sefa Marrin do?

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't hurry. He finishes the far side of the street and lets his eyes do the slow work on that closed shutter — what's below it, whether the window looks onto the Coast Way or back into the yard, where the stair to the rooms must come down from, given where the shop door sits.

Then he rounds the end of the board fence into whatever lane or gap runs behind it, hands loose, hood down, the look of a man checking he's got the right address. Back of the yard: is there a second door, a rear stair, a privy, a loose board or a gap a boy could squeeze through — and does the ground under any of it show feet that aren't the cooper's. If there's a drainpipe, a lean-to or a stack of staves under that one shut window, he notes how a man would get up it, and how he'd get down in a hurry.

He wants it all in his head before anyone knocks. Then he comes back round to the front and finds Bram and Sefa — at the gate, not inside it.

"Well?" he says to them quietly, as he arrives. "Did Vell say anything after I left that I ought to know? Because he had something stuck in his throat when you asked him, Sefa, and it wasn't rent."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I fold Odda’s letter and tuck it inside my coat. For a moment my jaw tightens.

Quietly to Sefa, without looking toward the bench: “Young fellow outside the pie hatch. Burn scars on his arms, white on his fingers. Watched us come out, followed Pell with his eyes. Now he’s watching the yard. Don’t stare.”

I walk with her toward the gate to meet Pell, keeping the watcher in the edge of my sight rather than confronting him.

Once we’re together and can speak without being overheard, I pass the warning to Pell, then show both of them the letter.

“This came just now. Changes things for me. I won’t slip a page out behind your backs—but I want to find out what’s happening to this house before we hand Vell the box.”

Bram doesn't turn his head. He speaks low at Sefa's shoulder while they walk, eyes on the cooper's gate, and the pie-seller's bench stays at the edge of his sight, where he put it. Sefa keeps to her own pace beside him. From the street the closed shutter looks no different from the others: weathered boards, a gap of a finger's width at the bottom where the frame has warped. Behind the gap there's only dark. The four open windows beside it show what lodgers' rooms show in the morning: a shirt drying on a sill, a jug, the corner of a bed.

Pell comes round the far end of the fence the way he left, at an idle pace. He has the yard in his head now. There's one stair, outside on the yard side, up to the gallery. The back gate is barred and hasn't been used. Behind it the lane mud lies smooth, with no prints but his own and a cart rut that's days old. The stave shed's roof sits under the shut window, a short step up for a man who climbs. And on the gatepost, knee-high, there's a chalk ring that wasn't drawn for the cooper's benefit. He reaches the front gate a moment after the other two and stops beside them, outside it, and asks his question quietly.

Bram passes his warning on first, in the same flat voice: the young man on the bench, burn-scarred arms, white on three fingers, watching the yard. Then he takes the folded letter out of his coat, opens it, and holds it low between the three of them so the street sees only a man checking a paper at a gate.

The hand is cramped and careful, and someone pressed hard enough to dent the page:

*Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold, and Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox — the one Vell has hired you to bring him. Jassan wrote to me before he died: once the box is back, Vell calls the note and takes the house. If that one page were gone before Vell opened the box, there would be nothing to call. Please. I have no one else to ask. — Odda Brand*

Bram says what he has to say over it and folds it away again.

Inside the yard Tobin's mallet stops. A broad, bald man in a leather apron straightens up over a half-hooped barrel and looks at the three of them across the yard: armour, a shield, a man who looks round corners for a living, a woman with prayer beads. He doesn't seem to mind them. He looks the way a man looks when he's guessed what they've come for and is glad it isn't his problem. Then he bends to the barrel again, and the mallet goes back to its thock and thock.

Up the street, at the edge of Bram's sight, the young man on the bench stands. He leaves the cold mug on the bench and heads south down the Coast Way, not hurrying, toward the far end of town. He's gone four steps when the pie-seller leans out of her hatch. "Oi! My mug!" He stops, turns red to the ears, comes back, and drains the cold stuff in one swallow. He hands the mug in through the hatch with a coin. Then he walks off south again, faster this time, and the traffic of the morning closes behind him.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell reads the letter once, doesn't touch it, and lets Bram fold it away. For a moment he just watches the young man with the burned fingers get smaller down the Coast Way.

"Well," he says, soft. "That's three days from a bad heart to a chalk mark."

He turns so his back is to the shop and his face to the two of them, like a man comparing the address on a paper. "Back gate's barred and unused — nobody's been through the lane but me. One outside stair, yard side, up to a gallery. Stave shed roof sits right under the shut window; a child could step from it onto the sill. And on the back gatepost, knee-high, there's a chalk ring. The cooper didn't draw it. That's cant — the Gate's cant, or near enough. It means this place is *spoken for*. Someone's marked it as a job, or marked it as done, or marked it to tell the next man along to keep his hands off." He shrugs one shoulder. "Which of the three, I can't say from a circle. But Vell said no one had asked him about the ledgers, and I believed his hands. Nobody needed to ask him. They asked the window."

He looks at Bram. "Your Odda's letter says Ferr wrote to her before he died. So Ferr knew what was in that box and who it would hurt. A clerk who knows that, and asks his master for his wage early ten days back, and is refused, and then dies in his chair —" He stops himself. "I'm not saying anything. I'm saying I'd like to be in that room before anyone else is in it again, and I'd like to go up the stair like honest men, with Wenna Pike, and not through the window — because whoever drew that circle may have left the window for us to find."

A beat. "As for the page. I'm a hired hand. I was hired to carry a box with the wax whole, and I'll carry it. But I'm not deaf, and the lad with the scarred fingers isn't either, and I'd say we're not the only ones who've heard there's forty gold in a sheet of paper. Let's see the box first. Then let's see whether there's still a page to argue about."

He nods toward the shop. "Bram, you knock — you've the note and the honest face. I'll stand where I can see the stair and the shed roof both."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“South,” I murmur to the others. “Same direction as Thale’s counting-room. Could mean nothing, but we may have company before long.”

I put the letter away and step through the gate, stopping clear of the cooper’s work.

“Morning. Looking for Wenna Pike. We’re here about Jassan Ferr’s strongbox, with a note from Vell. Where should we knock?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her eyes on the gate while Bram speaks, but her attention folds around the letter like a hand closing over a flame.

When he finishes, she is quiet for a moment. Then she says, low, "You were right to show us, and right not to do it quietly. If Vell's note for forty gold is in that box, it doesn't only explain the hour on him — it names the pressure." She glances down the street after the vanished young man, long gone into the morning traffic. "And the boy with the cold mug wasn't hired to watch a box. Hirelings don't redden at a pie-seller over a borrowed mug. He was cheap and curious." She lets out a small breath. "Which means someone else is cheap and curious, or he's someone's nervous errand boy. Either way, he'll report us."

She turns her face up toward the closed shutter, the one eye shut among the blinking windows. "That one," she says. "It's the only one latched. Could be Ferr's, or could be Tobin keeping sunlight off his stores. Wenna Pike will know." Her fingers find the beads under her sleeve and still. "I won't take any side yet, even a widow's. I need to see the room and the box before I believe any of it — Vell's story, Odda Brand's, or Jassan's." She says the dead clerk's name gently, like a patient's. "But if it's true, and one page is all that stands between a woman and her house... that is not a small thing to hand back sealed."

She looks to Pell, then to Bram. "Knock now. Two of us kind, one of us grieving or owed. I'd like to do the talking with the landlady, if you don't mind. She'll want payment, and I've spent years asking people for the truth in small rooms."

She starts toward the gate, but pauses just at the post and speaks over her shoulder, very softly. "And whatever we decide about the page, say nothing of the widow inside the yard. The wall has ears, and that dog won't be the only thing listening."

scenes.narration:
Tobin doesn't stop for Pell's murmur at the gate or Sefa's quiet words behind it. When Bram steps through into the yard and stands clear of the work, the cooper lands one more blow on the hoop, checks it with his thumb, and only then straightens up.

"Top of the stair. First door off the gallery." He points the mallet at the wooden steps climbing the side of the shop. "She'll have heard you. She hears everything in this yard."

He looks at the note-shaped bulge in Bram's coat, then up at the end window. "That's his. The shut one. He closed it himself back end of summer and never opened it again. Said the light came off the street wrong onto his figures." He shrugs, a big slow movement in the leather apron. "Walked the boards half the night, the last week or so. I'd hear him over my head, up and down. Then I didn't." He bends to the barrel again and says the rest to the oak. "Wasn't my business. Isn't now."

Pell has already picked his spot, just inside the gate where the stave stacks hide him from the street. From there he can see the stair, the gallery and the whole length of the shed roof under the end window. In daylight the roof tells him a plain story. Moss runs unbroken along the shingle joints, and a summer's worth of leaves and grit lies in the gutter. A season of rain has streaked the dust on the sill above it. Nobody has climbed to that window. Whoever drew the ring on the back post did it from the lane and went no further.

<<<
Pell Dunmore: Pell reads the letter once, doesn't touch it, and lets Bram fold it away. For a moment he just watches the young man with the burned fingers get smaller down the Coast Way.

"Well," he says, soft. "That's three days from a bad heart to a chalk mark."

He turns so his back is to the shop and his face to the two of them, like a man comparing the address on a paper. "Back gate's barred and unused — nobody's been through the lane but me. One outside stair, yard side, up to a gallery. Stave shed roof sits right under the shut window; a child could step from it onto the sill. And on the back gatepost, knee-high, there's a chalk ring. The cooper didn't draw it. That's cant — the Gate's cant, or near enough. It means this place is *spoken for*. Someone's marked it as a job, or marked it as done, or marked it to tell the next man along to keep his hands off." He shrugs one shoulder. "Which of the three, I can't say from a circle. But Vell said no one had asked him about the ledgers, and I believed his hands. Nobody needed to ask him. They asked the window."

He looks at Bram. "Your Odda's letter says Ferr wrote to her before he died. So Ferr knew what was in that box and who it would hurt. A clerk who knows that, and asks his master for his wage early ten days back, and is refused, and then dies in his chair —" He stops himself. "I'm not saying anything. I'm saying I'd like to be in that room before anyone else is in it again, and I'd like to go up the stair like honest men, with Wenna Pike, and not through the window — because whoever drew that circle may have left the window for us to find."

A beat. "As for the page. I'm a hired hand. I was hired to carry a box with the wax whole, and I'll carry it. But I'm not deaf, and the lad with the scarred fingers isn't either, and I'd say we're not the only ones who've heard there's forty gold in a sheet of paper. Let's see the box first. Then let's see whether there's still a page to argue about."

He nods toward the shop. "Bram, you knock — you've the note and the honest face. I'll stand where I can see the stair and the shed roof both."

Bram Halloway: “South,” I murmur to the others. “Same direction as Thale’s counting-room. Could mean nothing, but we may have company before long.”

I put the letter away and step through the gate, stopping clear of the cooper’s work.

“Morning. Looking for Wenna Pike. We’re here about Jassan Ferr’s strongbox, with a note from Vell. Where should we knock?”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa keeps her eyes on the gate while Bram speaks, but her attention folds around the letter like a hand closing over a flame.

When he finishes, she is quiet for a moment. Then she says, low, "You were right to show us, and right not to do it quietly. If Vell's note for forty gold is in that box, it doesn't only explain the hour on him — it names the pressure." She glances down the street after the vanished young man, long gone into the morning traffic. "And the boy with the cold mug wasn't hired to watch a box. Hirelings don't redden at a pie-seller over a borrowed mug. He was cheap and curious." She lets out a small breath. "Which means someone else is cheap and curious, or he's someone's nervous errand boy. Either way, he'll report us."

She turns her face up toward the closed shutter, the one eye shut among the blinking windows. "That one," she says. "It's the only one latched. Could be Ferr's, or could be Tobin keeping sunlight off his stores. Wenna Pike will know." Her fingers find the beads under her sleeve and still. "I won't take any side yet, even a widow's. I need to see the room and the box before I believe any of it — Vell's story, Odda Brand's, or Jassan's." She says the dead clerk's name gently, like a patient's. "But if it's true, and one page is all that stands between a woman and her house... that is not a small thing to hand back sealed."

She looks to Pell, then to Bram. "Knock now. Two of us kind, one of us grieving or owed. I'd like to do the talking with the landlady, if you don't mind. She'll want payment, and I've spent years asking people for the truth in small rooms."

She starts toward the gate, but pauses just at the post and speaks over her shoulder, very softly. "And whatever we decide about the page, say nothing of the widow inside the yard. The wall has ears, and that dog won't be the only thing listening."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I glance at Sefa and give her a small nod, leaving the talking to her. Quietly, close enough that only she hears: “I’ll cover the rent from my share. No need to leave the room shut while we run errands for Vell.”

I take out three gold and four silver, keeping them in my hand for now, and hold up Vell’s note for Wenna to see.

“May we come up?”

While Sefa speaks with her, I keep an eye on the yard entrance. I don’t draw a weapon or crowd the stairs.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps clear of the gatepost, into the yard but not far — just enough that she can speak without raising her voice over the mallet. She tips her face up to the gallery, hands open at her sides.

"Wenna Pike," she says, pleasant and steady, the way she used to greet a new patient's family at the door. "I'm Sefa Marrin. You've guessed right: we're here for the strongbox, with Vell's note. But we're not here to clean out a dead man's room, and I won't pretend his debts travel with the box. You say three gold and four silver — I've heard you. The note doesn't pay it, and I won't insult you by waving it like it does."

She glances once at the stave stacks where Pell waits, then back to the rail. "Before we argue over who clears the rent, I'd like to see the door and the box as they are. If the seal's whole, the rest is haggling. If it isn't, your price and Vell's note are both footnotes to a different story."

She pauses, and lets the mallet's beat fall once, twice. "And I'd rather not talk about a dead man's debts in the middle of the yard, where every hammer and harness and dog can hear us. Let me come up and speak with you at the door — just us two, if you'll have it. If you won't open it, that's your right. But I want to see the state of things before any coin changes hands."

Her voice drops a shade. "This Coll Brannock — did he show you silver or just show you teeth? And did he so much as touch the door? If he's already had his eye on that lock, the seal may not be Vell's anymore."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays where he is among the staves, and lets Sefa have the gallery. But he speaks low to the two of them, without taking his eyes off the stair.

"Three and four. That's a copper apiece against seventy-five, and Vell said to bring him the number — he didn't say not to pay it. I'll put in my third now and argue with him later. A week's a long time for a woman who's already had one offer, and I'd rather the door opened for us than for Coll Brannock." He's already working a few coins loose from his purse, keeping the rest out of sight. "Sefa — your show. But if you'd ask her two things for me: did Brannock go up those stairs, or stand where we're standing? And has anyone been through that door since the temple carried Ferr out — her, Tobin, anyone she lent the key to. I'd like to know whose boots I'm walking behind."

He watches the dog a moment, the way it won't look away from the stair. "And ask her what the dog's unhappy about. Dogs don't read notes."

He adds, barely a murmur, for Bram alone: "Coll Brannock talks like the Gate. So does that chalk ring. He drew it from the lane and never climbed — the moss on that roof hasn't been touched all summer. He's not a burglar. He's a buyer who marks his claim so the burglars stay off it. Which means whoever he answers to would rather have the box bought than stolen — for now."

Wenna's eyes go to Bram's hand before Sefa has said three words. She sees the coins in his palm and the paper held up beside them, and the coins are what she looks at. Then Sefa speaks, and the landlady's gaze moves to her and stays there. She hears her out with both hands on the rail. She doesn't interrupt, and her face doesn't soften.

"You're the first of Vell's lot to say his note doesn't pay," she says when Sefa has finished. "I'll give you that." She looks once more at Bram's fist and back again. "And you're right about the yard. I hear everything in it. So does everybody else."

She takes Sefa's questions in the order they came, flatly.

"Silver? Gold. He opened his purse on Tobin's chopping block and let me count what was in it, and it was a good deal more than three and four. That was his manners. He's got the other kind too. I could see them waiting behind his teeth." She jerks her chin down at the packed earth where Bram is standing. "Stood there. About where he is. Asked which door was Ferr's, and I told him, since it's no secret. He found the window by himself, just looking. He never set foot on my stair. I'd have heard him if he had. That stair talks."

Then the door. "It's locked with my lock, and the key's here." She puts a hand on the ring at her waist and doesn't swing it. "The box is on his table under the shut window, where he left it. Wax all down the crack of the lid. I didn't touch it. I've no use for a box I can't open." She stops there, her mouth thin. "As for seeing it before I'm paid. Seeing the box means opening the room, and the room is three and four. That's how it is, and it's no different for you than it was for him with the purse."

She steps back from the rail as far as her own doorway and stands holding the frame. Behind her are a scrubbed table, a kettle, and a window that looks straight down into the yard.

"Come up, then, if you want to talk where Tobin's barrels can't hear. You," she says to Sefa. "Bring that with you" — a nod at Bram's hand — "or bring him with it. I don't mind which. The other one can stop down there among the staves. He's been looking at my roof for a quarter of an hour."

The end door stands shut beside hers, a plain plank door with an iron hasp and a padlock as big as a fist. Nobody has painted it for years, and nobody has scratched it lately.

Under the shed's eave the brown dog gets up off its sack. It doesn't go toward the stair. It pulls its chain out to its full length toward the end of the gallery, stops, and gives one thin whine at the shut door above. Then it lies down again with its back to the yard. Tobin's mallet hasn't stopped. Out on the Coast Way a cart goes by toward the smithies, and from somewhere south, past the town's roofs, a bell is marking the hour.

Bram keeps to the open ground of the yard, sword sheathed, well back from the foot of the stair. All the while Wenna talks, he keeps the cart-wide gate in the corner of his eye. Through it the Coast Way goes about its morning: a carter, two smith's boys with a coal sack slung between them, a woman with a basket of eggs. None of them slows at the cooper's gate, and none of them looks in. The bench outside the pie-seller's hatch is empty, and no one has come to sit on it. For now nobody is watching the yard but the people already in it.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa looks up at Wenna for a long moment, then gives a small nod — the same grave, accepting nod she gave Vell. She turns to Bram without stepping closer to the stair.

"Let the rent be paid at the door," she says, low enough for him and no further. "But not into her hand, not yet. You carry it, and you come up with me. Pell has the yard."

Then she lifts her voice to the gallery. "My friend brings it. And I'll come up and speak with you, just us two at the door — though he'll stand at the stair's head where I can see him." She doesn't ask permission for the last part; she says it the way she'd have informed the hospice sister of where the night candle would be kept.

She begins up the stair, one hand just brushing the rail. Halfway, she pauses and looks back once — not at Pell, but at the brown dog, now lying with its back to the yard. Her mouth tightens. Then she climbs the rest of the way, stops well short of Wenna's doorway, and folds her hands in front of her. In the enclosed space of the gallery her voice is gentler, but no less precise.

"Brannock opened a purse and found out your windows. I don't like the order he did things in." Her eyes travel to the padlocked door and its hasp. "The dog knows which room is that one, and it isn't because of the smell of old ledgers. Did the dog keen like that while Ferr was dying? While Brannock was standing in your yard?"

She lets a beat pass. "I ask because I used to sit with the dying, in a hospice down in the Gate. Dogs take a room's measure before the rest of us do. That door isn't haunted, though. It's only locked." She tips her head toward the hasp. "While Bram pays you, I'll look at that hasp and the frame — nothing more, not the room. If someone's broken in since Ferr died, you'll want to know before you let the next blackguard through."

She waits, calm, leaving the air for Wenna to answer or refuse.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lifts a hand to the gallery, open-palmed — caught, and not minding. "It's a good roof," he calls up, mild. "Nobody's been on it. That's a compliment to your gutters, mistress, not an insult to your door."

Then he pulls a gold piece and two silver from his purse and steps out just far enough to put them in Bram's hand on his way past. "My third. Take it up with the note. If she wants to count it on the table, let her — that's manners."

Lower, to Sefa as she passes him toward the stair: "The dog went to the *end* door, not the stair. Not to her, not to us — to Ferr's room. There's something on the other side of that plank it doesn't like, and it's been three days. Could be nothing worse than a dead man's smell in a shut room. Could be a cat. Ask her if the dog's done that since the temple came. And ask her for the key to the padlock, not to come down and open it herself — I'd like to be the one who turns it. If the hasp's been pulled and reset I'll feel it before I see it."

He stays where she told him, among the staves — but he shifts a pace so the padlock on the end door is square in his view, and lets his eyes settle on it: how the hasp sits in the wood, whether the screws are bright or rusted with the plate, whether the lock hangs the way a lock hangs when it was last closed by a woman's hand at her own height or by a man's reaching across. The rest of his attention he gives to the gate and the stretch of Coast Way beyond it, and to the quarter where the bench stands empty — because a boy who ran south at that pace will be coming back, or someone will be coming in his place.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, keep an eye on the gate. Dog’s uneasy about that end room, too.”

I go up with Sefa and offer Wenna the three gold and four silver.

“That clears Ferr’s rent through today? I’d like a receipt, please. Bram Halloway paid it—not Vell.”

Once she accepts, I leave Sefa room to talk and look along the gallery toward Ferr’s door, listening for anything from inside.

“Has the dog been doing that since Ferr died?”

scenes.narration:
Wenna watches the three of them work it out below her. Pell's coins go into Bram's palm on the way past. Sefa says something low that the yard doesn't catch. Then the two of them start up the stair. Pell's compliment about the gutters gets no more from her than a short look down at the staves.

"Tobin's gutters," she says. "Thank Tobin."

The stair talks just as she promised: every tread gives its own complaint under Bram's chain mail. Sefa climbs ahead of him, one hand on the rail. Halfway up she looks back at the dog, and it is still lying with its back to the yard. At the top she stops well short of Wenna's doorway. Bram stops at the head of the stair, where Sefa can see him, and holds out the coins on his open hand, three gold and four silver.

Wenna counts them without picking them up, moving each one with a fingertip. Then she takes them all at once and drops them into her apron pocket.

"Receipt," she says, as if Bram had asked her for something odd. "You'll have one. I'll put down who paid, and gladly." She goes inside and comes back with a stub of pencil and the torn-off flap of a flour sack. She writes on the doorframe, slowly, pressing hard: *Had of Bram Halloway 3 gold 4 silver. Rent of J. Ferr paid to the day he died. Not from Vell. W. Pike.* She hands it to him. "Paid to the day he died. Not through today. From today the room's mine again. You've till dark to get his box out of it. The bed and the rest stop here. That's custom, and your paper doesn't say otherwise."

Then she answers the dog, Bram's question and Sefa's together, because to her it's all one question.

"He fed it. Every night after his supper he'd come out on this gallery and drop it the rind off his cheese, and of a morning too, going out. Since the temple took him it goes to his door at those hours. Morning and supper." She doesn't look down at the yard. "Night he died it howled till Tobin threw a boot at it. I took it for a fox about the midden. It growled at your Brannock the way it growled at you. It growls at everybody. Everybody but Jassan."

Sefa turns to the end door, and Wenna lets her look. The hasp is old iron, and its screws went in long ago and were painted over with the plank. The paint across their heads is cracked with age and nothing else. No screwdriver has turned them, and nobody has levered the hasp. The padlock is Wenna's, a big black lump of a thing.

"Nobody's broke in," Wenna says. "I'd know. I've been in, airing it. That's all." Beside her the end shutter stays shut, its warped bottom edge a dark line, just as it has been all morning.

Bram stands at the head of the stair and listens along the gallery to the plank door. No sound comes from behind it. No board shifts, and nothing moves. Something comes under the door, though, faint in the still air of the gallery: a smell of cold ash, and under it something bitter and green, like a physick left uncorked.

From his place among the staves Pell has the padlock square in his view, and what he sees is what Sefa sees up close. The paint on the screws is unbroken. The lock hangs straight down, at a small woman's reach, the way it was last snapped shut. Whatever the dog is waiting for, nobody has come through that door by force. Past the cart gate the Coast Way goes about its morning. A cart of charcoal goes by, then a girl with geese, and no one comes back up the street from the south.

Wenna takes the key ring from her waist and picks one key out without having to look. She fits it to the padlock. It opens with a heavy iron click, and she hooks it open on the hasp and steps back. The plank door is still shut, but it's unlocked now.

"Paid's paid," she says.

Down in the yard the brown dog gets up off its sack at the sound of the lock and stands at the end of its chain. It isn't whining now. It just watches the end of the gallery.

 Neither action needed a roll, and both were played in the turn: Sefa climbed the stair with Bram behind her carrying the coin, and her look at the hasp showed an undisturbed door, with old paint unbroken over the screws and nobody's forced entry to find.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I tuck the receipt away. “Thank you.”

To Sefa, quietly: “Cold ash and something bitter under the door. Like medicine. Let’s leave bottles and cups where they are.”

I shift my shield onto my arm and stand to one side of the doorway. “Opening it.”

I lift the latch and ease the door open without stepping across the threshold, looking over the floor immediately inside before the rest of the room. I keep clear enough for Sefa to see past me.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa gives Wenna a small, grave nod. "Paid, then. I'll open it. Neither of us so much as shifts the box until I've seen the wax." She glances back at Bram without fully turning. "Watch the stair, not me. If someone comes up, call out."

She steps to the side of the end door, out of the frame, and looks first at the threshold, then at the hinge side, then sets her fingertips against the planks and pushes the door open slowly, letting the daylight from the gallery fall in ahead of her. She does not cross at once.

Instead she cups one hand over her prayer beads and murmurs a word too low for the yard to hear. A small, warm light kindles between her fingers, white-gold and steady. She opens her hand and lets it wash into the room: the floor, the bed, the chair, the table under the shut window, the shape of the box upon it, the dark line of the window catch.

Then, without turning, she says to Wenna, "When you aired it, what did you touch? Did you open that shutter? Dust the table?" Her voice is calm, but her eyes move slowly, reading the room's shadows before she trusts them with her feet.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell watches the padlock swing open on its hasp and lets out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. Then he leaves the staves and crosses the yard, giving the dog a wide, unhurried berth — and takes the stair at the edge of the treads, where the nails are, so it complains less under him than it did under Bram.

At the top he stops beside the other two and keeps his voice down.

"Screws are painted over, lock hung straight. Nobody's forced that door. Whatever the dog's about, it came in by invitation or it was already inside." He nods to Wenna, civil. "Mistress — obliged. One thing more, and I'll ask it plain since the yard hears everything anyway: has the dog been doing that since the temple carried him out? Standing at the end there, watching this door?"

Then, to Sefa and Bram: "Let me go first. Not for the box — for the floor. If a man walked the boards half the night in his last week, I'd like to see where he walked before three pairs of feet go over it."

He eases the plank door inward a hand's width with his fingertips, not his palm, and stops there — nose, then ears, then eyes. The smell of a shut room three days closed: whether it's only stale, or whether it's something the dog has reason to mind. Any sound. Then the strip of floor just inside the threshold — dust, a dropped thing, a mark — before he pushes it wide and steps in along the wall, leaving the middle of the room untrodden.

screens.Pell Dunmore:

At the top you find the end door already standing open against the inside wall. Daylight lies across the floorboards, and a white-gold light from Sefa's beads shines at the sill. You don't need to ease the door; the room is there to read.

You put your questions to Wenna, and she answers from her own doorway without stepping out. The dog was fed morning and supper, she says, and it goes and stands there at those hours. It is doing it now because the lock is open. She looks down at the yard and back again. "It's a dog. It doesn't know he's gone."

You give the room your nose first. It smells of cold ash and of the bitter green physick, strongest over by the nightstand. Under those is what a shut room keeps of a man: old wool, lamp-black, ink. Nothing has gone off in here, and there is no sweetness of rot. Then you listen. Out in the yard Tobin's mallet goes thock, and inside nothing answers it. The strip of floor inside the sill has been swept like the rest. The broom arcs curve round things, and nothing lies dropped on the boards.

You step in along the wall with your shoulder near the plaster. You leave the middle of the room alone and watch the boards as you go.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stands in the doorway with the light running silver along the boards. She says nothing at once. Her gaze moves slowly: the swept arcs in the dust, the stained boards under the nightstand, the cold grate with its half-curled scrap of paper, the chair pushed back at its angle, and the box in the light with its lid shut and its seam of wax.

Her face doesn't change, but the prayer beads go still in her fingers and she steps a little aside so the gallery's light and her own fall together on the table. "That's not Vell's red," she says quietly, more to herself than to Wenna. "It's green as bottle glass, and I've never seen Ostrin Vell's hand with green wax. His mark is scales and a V."

She looks to Bram without turning her head. "I'm not crossing till I know the room isn't lying to us." Then, louder, still steady: "Wenna, you swept round the table and the stain. A careful kind of kindness, sweeping around a dead man's things." The words are soft, without judgment.

She raises her free hand, fingers slight, the light bobbing as she does, so the room's corners lean and settle. "The shutter. He wanted it shut because the streetlight fell wrong onto his figures, Tobin said. Then the dust over the hook and the eye hasn't been cut by the hook moving in months, so the shutter hasn't been opened since."

She turns her face back to the room. "A sealed box, but green wax where the note says red. A written scrap half-burned in the fire. A spill by the bed no one has scrubbed. A man who walked the boards at night and then didn't. This isn't a simple chest to carry; this is a room that's been arranged, and the person who wants the box may already have walked through it once with a coin in his hand."

She looks to Bram with a question clear in her eyes: whether to enter now, or call Pell, or keep the room as it stands and mark what can't be trusted.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Green wax. Vell said red.” I keep my voice low. “We’ll want a proper look at that mark.”

I leave the doorway clear for Sefa and take watch at the stairhead, where I can see Pell and the yard entrance.

“Wenna, was that vial open and the spill there when you found him? And who told you his heart had failed?”

When I can catch Pell’s eye, I beckon him toward the foot of the stairs. “Box is here. Seal doesn’t match Vell’s description. Sefa’s looking it over; I’ve got the stair.”

scenes.narration:
Wenna listens to Sefa from her own doorway with her arms folded over her apron. The word *kindness* gets nothing from her face. "Swept round it because it's his," she says. "And because it wouldn't come up, and I'd better things to do with a brush than scrub at it for nothing."

Sefa's light holds steady over the table. From the sill, the round mark in the middle of the green seam is a pale dimple in the wax, too small to read. The dust strung between the shutter hook and its eye doesn't stir in the draught from the door. Nobody has lifted that hook since the webs were spun.

Bram leaves the doorway to Sefa and takes the head of the stair, where the gallery rail lets him see the whole yard and the cart gate beyond it. He asks his two questions over his shoulder, and Wenna answers him the way she has answered everything this morning: straight out, without moving from where she stands.

"Just like that, it was. Stopper out, the wet on the boards, him in the chair with his chin down on his chest, the candle burnt out." She tips her head at the nightstand without looking at it. "Drops. From the temple, the Song of the Morning, for his chest. He'd had a bottle off them since spring. Bitter as sin, he said, and it was meant to be." She stops, then gives the second answer, and for the first time she sounds a little short with someone. "Who told me his heart. Two brothers from the temple came for him in a handcart. The older one put his hand on him and looked at the bottle and said *his heart*. And I didn't need any telling. He'd come up those stairs grey in the face all summer, stopping halfway like an old man. He was thirty." She unfolds her arms. "Nobody poisoned that boy, if that's where you're going. Nobody came up my stair to do it."

Down in the yard, the place among the staves where Pell stood is empty. Bram's beckoning hand finds nobody to answer it. Tobin works on with his back to the gallery, thock and thock. The brown dog sits square on the packed earth with its eyes on the open door. Through the cart gate the Coast Way runs on as before: a smith's boy with a barrow of scrap, two women arguing over a basket, a mule. Nobody slows at the gate. Above it the sun has climbed clear of the roofs across the street and lies warm and yellow on the gallery boards, right up to the threshold of the dead man's room, and stops there.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't touch it yet. He crouches at the wall, well off the pale track, and looks at the board the way he'd look at a lock — the gap, the two bright nail heads, the two thumb-and-finger smudges at the wall end.

"Sefa. Bram." Barely above the mallet. "Don't come across the middle — come round by the wall, if you come at all. And Bram, if you'd stand in the doorway a moment with your back to the room. Not to keep the mistress out — to keep the yard from seeing what we're looking at. The box is where she said. This isn't the box."

He points with one finger, not touching. "He walked chair to grate, grate to chair, and turned here every time. Every nail in this floor's gone grey but these two, and these have been lifted and pushed back by hand more than once. Dust on the ends, and his thumb and finger in it where he prised it. A man doesn't do that in his last week for a spare key." He glances up at Sefa. "Whatever the chalk man wants, and whatever Odda's letter's about — I'd say Ferr already took it out of the box and put it under his floor. Which would be why the wax is whole."

Then, to the board. He draws one dagger, tests the proud edge first with the flat of the blade for anything that gives or clicks wrong, and only then slips the point under the lifted end and eases it up an inch — slow, enough to see into the gap before he sees what's in it. If it's only a cavity and paper, he lifts it clear and sets it on the hearthstone, and looks before he reaches.

scenes.narration:
Pell's voice carries no further than the door, low under Tobin's mallet. Whether anyone comes round by the wall is up to the people on the gallery. He keeps his eyes on the board.

He runs the flat of the dagger along the proud edge first, from the wall end to the grate end. Nothing gives or clicks, and there's no wire or pin under it. It's an old board over a gap, and nothing has been fixed to it but its own two nails. He knows how this should feel, and it feels the way a board feels. He works the point in under the lifted end, at the smudges, and eases it up an inch.

The nails come with it at once. Someone has drawn them so often that the holes have gone loose, and they rise in the wood without a squeak. Through the gap Pell sees dark, dry space between two joists, about a hand deep. The light from the doorway slants in after his blade. There's no fluttering paper and no stack of sheets, only dust that has lain undisturbed except in one place.

He lifts the board clear and lays it on the hearthstone, nails up.

The cavity is the length of his forearm and holds one thing, set in the middle where a hand reaching down from the corner would find it without looking: a small bundle of oilcloth, folded tight and tied with brown thread. It's the size of a man's fist and heavy for its size, judging by how it presses into the dust under it. One end is rounded, and the other narrows like a short handle. Around it the dust is wiped into a smooth ring, the mark of something lifted out and put back many times, always in the same spot.

On the knot of the thread there's a smear no bigger than a fingernail. It's dark green, the colour of old bottle-glass, and it has dried hard and shiny.

The rest of the cavity is empty all the way to the joists. There are no papers. Out in the yard the mallet goes thock, then thock again. The light from the door falls steadily into the hole and across the green-smeared knot.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’m not saying he was poisoned, Wenna. Better to ask than make a story of it. Thank you.”

To Sefa, low: “Pell’s stepped away. I’ll keep watch. Go carefully, but have your look at the seal and that scrap without shifting the box. Different wax doesn’t yet tell us who changed it—or when.”

I stay at the stairhead and scan the yard, including the shed and gate, for Pell or any sign of someone arriving. I call down to the cooper in an ordinary voice: “Tobin, did you see which way our companion went?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa shakes her head, once, not in denial but in reassurance. "I don't think anyone came up your stair, Wenna. Nobody needed to." She lets that lie where it falls.

Then she steps across the threshold at last, slowly, her bead-light leading, and the boards answer under her weight with small dry creaks. She walks the long way round, not past the stain, and stops first at the cold grate. She goes down into a crouch, setting her free hand on her knee, and studies the half-burnt scrap where it curls from the ash.

"Bram, watch the yard. If Pell makes for the stair, call up before he puts a foot on it." Her voice is low, intent. "I want to know what Jassan burned, and whether he meant to." She lifts one hand before her, fingers open, and a pale, shadowless hand of her own light detaches from the lamp-glow and drifts forward. It takes the scrap by its white corner with exacting care, as a sister might lift a fallen petal from a sickbed, and carries it through the air to Sefa's waiting palm. The air tastes of ash.

Only then does she rise, turning the scrap so the light falls across its careful writing, and her eyes move along the line of it. "And then I'll know if the green wax belongs to the boy or to the man with the purse."

scenes.narration:
Wenna hears Bram out from her doorway with her arms folded again. "Ask, then," she says. "Asking's free." Sefa's quieter line, *nobody needed to*, reaches her too. Her eyes narrow at it for a moment, and then she lets it go without a word. She stays where she is, half in her own door, watching.

Bram keeps the head of the stair. From the rail he can see the whole yard. There are the pale stave stacks where Pell stood, and the stretch of earth between them and the fence is empty now. He sees the shed roof with its moss unbroken, the dog sitting square on its sack, and the cart gate and the strip of Coast Way beyond it. Two smith's boys go past with a coal sack, then a carter walking at his mule's head. Nobody turns in and nobody slows.

He calls down in an ordinary voice. Tobin finishes the stroke, sets the mallet on the barrel's rim and turns half round, wiping his scalp with the back of his wrist.

"Didn't see. Had my back to it." He glances at the staves, then up at Bram, and his face doesn't change. "He's quiet on his feet, that one. Wasn't by the gate, I'd have seen the gate." He picks the mallet up again. Thock.

Inside, Sefa crosses the sill at last. The boards give their small dry complaints under her as she goes the long way round, along the bed and past the pegs, keeping clear of the dark stain under the nightstand. The bitter green smell thickens as she passes it and thins again by the hearth. She sinks into a crouch before the grate with one hand on her knee, and her bead-light falls full into the ash.

It's more ash than one supper fire would leave. It lies in a fine grey heap that has kept its layers: flakes stacked thin as leaves, some of them still holding the faint ruled lines of a page before they crumble. A good many sheets went into this grate, and burned well. The scrap she came for is the one that didn't. It curls up out of the front of the heap, where it must have slid off the top as the rest caught, browned along the edge and white at the corner.

She lifts her free hand. The pale spectral hand slips forward out of the glow, takes the scrap by its white corner and draws it up out of the ash. It doesn't hurry, and the brittle edge holds. It carries the scrap through the air and lays it in her open palm.

The writing is small and careful, a clerk's hand, the same hand that laid the pen square on the table. Scorching has taken most of the sheet. What's left are three pieces of lines. At the top, in letters a little larger than the rest, as a man writes when he's addressing someone:

*—to Sergeant Cowl, of the Fist, at the—*

Lower down, in the middle of what was once a longer line, the words are perfectly clear:

*—the notes were sold before the wagons—*

At the bottom, along the burnt edge, half a line runs off into brown:

*—I cannot say who he is, only that he signs himself—*

There the paper is gone. The rest of the line is ash in the grate behind her with the other pages, one more flake among the many.

In the doorway the white-gold light of the beads lies across the floor. Out in the yard the mallet goes thock and thock, and the dog hasn't taken its eyes off the open door.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell goes very still, the way he does when a lock turns one notch sooner than it should.

"Not paper," he says, under the mallet. "Heavy. And the knot's got the same green on it as the bottle by his bed — I can smell it from here. So he tied this with physick on his fingers, and he tied it more than once."

He doesn't reach in with his hand. He slides the dagger's flat under the bundle at the handle end and tips it up out of the dust onto the blade, then onto the hearthstone beside the board, so it lies in the light. He wipes the dagger on his sleeve before he sheathes it — he's not touching that green with skin.

"Sefa — you were hospice. Come look at this smear before I open anything. If that's what I think it is, I'd like to know whether it's the kind that's bitter in a cup or the kind that's bitter under a nail." He keeps his own fingers back and uses the point of his second dagger to tease one turn of the oilcloth loose at the rounded end — just enough to see what's inside, not enough to spill it. "Bram, the door, still. Whatever this is, it's what the chalk man came for, and the yard doesn't need to know we've found it."
