scenes.narration:
Pell slides the flat of the dagger under the narrow end of the bundle and lifts it out of the dust. It sits heavy on the blade, as heavy as it looked. He tips it onto the hearthstone next to the board, where the light falls full on it, then wipes the steel on his sleeve and sheathes it. His words to the other two go no further than the doorway. Tobin's mallet in the yard drowns everything else.

In the light, the green smear on the knot isn't what a spill leaves. A dried drop of physick sinks into thread and stains it. This one stands up off the thread instead: a small hard bead, glossy on top, with a crisp edge where it cooled. One side is flattened, as if a thumb pressed it while it was still soft. It's the colour of old bottle-glass, the same green as the line down the strongbox's seam, only a few feet away on the table. The room's bitter smell hangs everywhere, thickest over by the nightstand. Down here by the cold grate, with his face close to the knot, Pell smells oilcloth, dust and old ash. He can't smell anything on the bead.

He sets the point of his second dagger under the outermost fold at the rounded end and works it loose. The oilcloth is stiff with age and gives way slowly, and one turn peels back from what's inside.

Inside is metal, dull grey and soft-looking, too heavy for its size to be anything but lead. It's the edge of a flat round face about the width of two fingers, cut smooth and true like a coin's rim. Just inside the rim, an engraved line runs into the cloth that still covers the rest. It's shallow and curved, and it could be part of a letter, a picture or a border. The groove isn't clean. Tiny green flecks sit packed into the bottom of the cut, the same glossy green as the bead on the knot. Something warm was pressed against this face, and not all of it came away.

The bundle lies on the hearthstone with that one turn open and the rest still wrapped. The board lies beside it, nails up, and next to that is the empty hole with its smooth ring in the dust. In the yard the mallet goes thock, then thock again.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays crouched at the grate a moment longer, the slip of paper resting across her fingers. Her lips move silently, once, over the words. Then she rises and crosses to the doorway just far enough for Bram to see the scrap, turning it so the scatter of lines catches the light. She keeps her voice low, meant only for him.

"It's not a ledger page. It's a letter — or the draft of one. To a sergeant of the Fist named Cowl." She tilts the paper slightly. "The bit in the middle: *the notes were sold before the wagons.* And at the bottom: *I cannot say who he is, only that he signs himself—* Then the fire took the rest." She looks at him steadily. cards.title: Religion (Intelligence +1, proficiency +3): does Sefa know the scales over a closed eye?

presses.text:
The light holds steady, and Sefa studies the mark until her eyes ache. She knows she has seen something shaped like it, in some margin or under some engraving — but the memory stays just out of reach, like a face in a crowd that is gone before you turn. The scales hang level. The eye beneath them is shut, and the curl of its lash-line is exact.

She lets out a slow breath and straightens, not touching the box. "I can't name it," she says, so only Bram and Wenna at the doorway can hear. "The scales are balanced. The eye is closed, not sleeping — shut on purpose. It's a sign someone meant to leave on this box, in Vell's stead, for anyone who got this far." Her voice is quiet, but it carries the particular heaviness of a healer forced to say she doesn't know. "It isn't any god I was ever taught to read."

She steps back from the table, carefully, so the hem of her sleeve doesn't brush the wax, and looks down at the floor around the chair and table. The broom's careful arcs have left a margin of dust there too: untouched, like a chalk line drawn around the whole end of the room. Around the table legs, the arcs show where Wenna's broom stopped short of the box and the chair. They show nothing else. No scuff. No heel-print. No scatter of dust where a second man might have braced his foot while leaning over the lock.

"The room's gone quiet," Sefa says, as if testing the thought. "Too quiet for a death and a sealed chest and a burned letter." She looks back over her shoulder toward the gallery, and Bram, and the empty yard now missing one quick shadow. "One eye shut above the bed; another on the box. It feels less like an accident and more like a message left for someone still walking."

Then she slips the half-burnt scrap into an inner fold of her coat, and raises her voice a little to Wenna. "If you'd let us, I'd like my friend Pell to see the room as it stands before we take the strongbox down. It may be that we need clear eyes and a second pair of hands." She turns her face toward the stairhead, and for the first time lets her worry show. "If he's gone far — call for him. Quietly, not at the top of your lungs."

+ Where the seal's mark sits — as a note, no changes to counters.
? The green mark is a pair of scales over a closed eye. Sefa does not know it.

scenes.narration:
Bram's question to Wenna carries along the gallery. She doesn't come out of her doorway to answer it.

"It was the colour it is now. I didn't look at it any closer than I'd look at a stranger's boots. Wax is wax, and it wasn't mine to break." She shifts her shoulder against the frame. "The brothers didn't touch it. The young one asked whose it was. The old one said *not ours*, and they lifted Jassan out of the chair and went. The bottle stopped where it was, and so did the box."

Sefa's low words reach Bram as he glances back: a letter to a Fist sergeant named Cowl, *the notes were sold before the wagons*, *only that he signs himself—*, and then the burnt edge. Then she goes the long way round the stain to the table and stops just left of the chair, so her shadow falls clear of the box. She raises the beads. Her light runs down the seam from one end to the other and settles on the round mark in the middle.

At this distance the mark reads plainly. It isn't a balance over a V. It's a pair of scales with the pans hanging level, and beneath them a single eye, drawn shut: one curved lid with a fringe of short strokes for lashes. The impression is crisp and deep, pressed hard into the wax while it was soft.

Sefa searches her memory for where she has seen that sign before.

She can't place it. The scales she could hang on any counter in the Gate: moneylenders, guild weights, half the merchant marks on the docks. The shut eye under them belongs to none of those, and nothing from the hospice chapel or the shrines she knew comes back to her. Whoever owned this sign, it isn't a mark she was ever taught.

There's something else, though, that only shows when the light lies close and steady. Under the glossy skin of the wax runs a faint grain, fine curved lines whorled like the pad of a thumb. They aren't on the surface where a thumb would leave them. They sit deeper, inside the green, and they take her light differently from the wax around them: a little brighter, a little slower, as if the light had to go further in to reach them.

Then Sefa's palms grow warm. It isn't the warmth of the beads. It's the old warmth, the one from the ninth night on the ward. With it comes a feeling she knows: the light in her hand isn't finished. It could press on through the green and under the lid to the first page lying there, and further still, out along something thin that runs from this seal to somewhere she can't see.

*Only a little more owed.*

The warmth stays in her hands. The wax sits under her light, whole, and the closed eye stays closed.

Out on the gallery, Bram has the rail and the street, and the street has changed. From the south, a couple of hundred feet off and coming up the Coast Way at a walking pace, are two men he knows one of. The broad young smith with the burn-scarred forearms is back. Half a step ahead of him walks a lean man in a good brown coat, bareheaded, hands loose at his sides, who looks at the shop fronts as he passes like a man pricing them. He isn't hurrying, and he isn't looking for an address. He's looking at the cooper's gate as if he's been through it before. The young man says something to him and points with his chin toward the yard. The lean man nods once without turning his head. In the yard, Tobin's mallet comes down again, thock, and the brown dog gets up off its sack.

The impression is crisp and deep, pressed hard into the wax while it was soft.

She can't place it. The scales she could hang on any counter in the Gate: moneylenders, guild weights, half the merchant marks on the docks. The shut eye under them belongs to none of those, and nothing from the hospice chapel or the shrines she knew comes back to her. Whoever owned this sign, it isn't a mark she was ever taught.

There's something else, though, that only shows when the light lies close and steady. Under the glossy skin of the wax runs a faint grain, fine curved lines whorled like the pad of a thumb. They aren't on the surface where a thumb would leave them. They sit deeper, inside the green, and they take her light differently from the wax around them: a little brighter, a little slower, as if the light had to go further in to reach them.

It could press on through the green and under the lid to the first page lying there, and further still, out along something thin that runs from this seal to somewhere she can't see.

*Only a little more owed.*

The warmth stays in her hands. The wax sits under her light, whole, and the closed eye stays closed.

Out on the gallery, Bram has the rail and the street, and the street has changed. From the south, a couple of hundred feet off and coming up the Coast Way at a walking pace, are two men he knows one of. The broad young smith with the burn-scarred forearms is back. In the yard, Tobin's mallet comes down again, thock, and the brown dog gets up off its sack.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets out a short breath through his nose — not quite a laugh.

"Not poison," he says, low. "Wax. Sealing wax, green, and this is what it was pressed with." He turns the dagger point so the light catches the flecks in the groove. "Lead, cut like a coin face, with a device on it. That's a seal die. A clerk doesn't keep one of those under his floor for his own letters — he keeps it because it isn't his device."

He peels the rest of the oilcloth back with the dagger, one turn at a time, until the whole face lies up in the light — he wants the picture. Scales and a V, or something else entirely. He keeps his skin off it; lead and wax both take a thumbprint.

"Sefa. The box. Don't touch it — just tell me what colour the wax is on that lid seam. Vell said red, scales and a V. From here I'm seeing green on the seam and green in this groove, and that's two greens too many for one dead man's room." He glances toward the door. "Bram — if it's green on that box, then the seal that's *whole* isn't Vell's, and someone's hoping he won't look close. Or someone's hoping we won't. Either way, this little coin stays with us until we know whose face is on it."

scenes.narration:
Pell peels the oilcloth back with the point of the dagger, one stiff turn after another, and never lets his skin touch it. The cloth comes away in its own folded shape. On the last turn the whole thing tips over and lies face up on the hearthstone in the light.

It's a seal die, as he guessed: a squat lead stamp the size of a fist. A short shank comes off one end to make a handle, and the round face at the other end is about two fingers across. The device is cut deep into the face, reversed the way a die has to be so the impression comes out the right way round. It isn't a balance with a V. It's a pair of scales with the pans hanging level, and under them a single eye, drawn shut. The lid is one curved line, and a fringe of short strokes below it makes the lashes. Green wax is packed into the bottom of every groove, in the pans, the beam and the lashes. Someone has pressed this into hot wax and put it away without cleaning it.

Two more things show once the face is clear of the cloth.

A ring of tiny letters runs round the rim, cut finer than the device and worn nearly smooth in places. Pell knows the Common hand, the cant marks of the Wide and the scrawl on a dockside bill of lading. These letters are none of those. To him they're only a pattern.

The other is on the end of the shank, where a hand would hold it. It isn't rounded off like a tool handle. It's filed flat, with a small square notch cut into one edge, crisp and deliberate. It looks like the half of a joint, made to fit against something else that isn't here.

The white-gold light from the doorway lies steady over the hearth. Where it falls into the cut lines of the device, the grooves take it slowly. They come up a shade brighter than the dull lead around them, a moment after the rest, as if the light had to travel further to reach the bottom of the cut. Nothing else in the room does that. The board, the hearthstone and the dagger's steel all take the light the ordinary way.

Pell's words to the other two go no further than the room, under the noise of the yard.

Then the yard changes. Tobin's mallet comes down once, and the next stroke doesn't come. Under the shed's eave the brown dog starts a low, steady growl, the one Wenna said it gives everybody, and its chain drags taut across the packed earth toward the cart gate.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Sefa. Watcher’s back, with a lean fellow in a brown coat. Couple of hundred feet off. Keep at the seal; I’ll meet them below.”

I turn to Wenna. “Is that Brannock?”

I head down the stairs, shield on my arm and sword sheathed, and take a position near the foot where anyone going up would have to pass me. I leave the gate clear and don’t call out to the men. As I cross the yard, I look once more for Pell.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa feels it like a hand turning over inside her own palms, and for one long moment she stands very still, the light from the beads brightening against her knuckles as if it would lean out of her toward the wax. Her lips part. The old impulse is there, warm as a lamp lit in a sickroom: *to see*.

Then she closes her fingers over the beads. It is a deliberate movement, unhurried, the way you close a patient's door so as not to wake them.

"No," she breathes, so low that only the box and the shut shutter could hear. "Not that way. It isn't ours to open."

She steps back one pace from the table, and the light in her hands dims to its ordinary gold — enough to see by, no more. The keen bright pressure drains from the seam of the wax, though the warmth stays stubbornly in the pads of her fingers, as if waiting. She flexes them once, gently, and it recedes, or seems to.

To Bram, without turning, she says in a low clear voice: "The mark is no one's I was ever taught. But the wax isn't dead. There's a grain in it — like light falling into water, but deeper. My light knew it." She pauses and chooses her words with care. "It wanted to go in. I told it no. Whatever runs from that seal ends somewhere I don't care to follow on a stranger's errand."

She turns then and puts her back to the box, looking past Bram toward the yard and the empty stave-stacks. "There's two things in this room that don't belong to Jassan: the green seal and the quiet." Her voice steadies back into its usual gentleness. "Let's have Pell up to read the quiet. And if he doesn't answer in another four hammers of Tobin's mallet, I'll call for him myself."

scenes.narration:
Sefa closes her fingers over the beads. The light in the room settles back to an ordinary lamp-gold, enough to see by and no more. The wax lies under it whole, the scales level and the eye shut. What she says to Bram goes out through the open door, low and clear.

He has already turned from the rail. At his question Wenna steps out of her doorway for the first time that morning and comes to the gallery rail. She looks down the length of the yard to the cart gate.

"That's him. Brannock. Same coat." Her mouth goes thin. "Didn't care to wait the week, then."

The stair complains at every tread under Bram's chain mail. He comes down with the shield on his arm and the sword in its sheath, and stops a pace out from the bottom step, where anyone going up would have to go past him. As he crosses the yard he looks over the stave stacks again. Pell isn't among them. Tobin has set his mallet on the barrel rim and stands with both hands on it, watching the gate. Nobody is making any strokes. Up in the dead man's room, the hammer-count Sefa meant to keep has nothing to count. Under the shed's eave the brown dog keeps up its low growl, its chain stretched taut toward the street.

The young smith stops outside the gate and leans on the post with his scarred arms folded. The lean man comes on in alone. He walks unhurried across the packed earth and stops about thirty feet short of Bram. He looks him over the way he priced the shop fronts: the mail, the shield, the hand kept clear of the hilt. His glance goes past Bram to the end of the gallery, where gold light spills out of the open door, and comes back again.

"Mistress Pike." He tips his head up to the rail. His voice is all the Gate, round in the vowels and flat at the ends.

"It's not mine to sell, Master Brannock," Wenna says. "It's paid for. Talk to them."

He takes that with a small nod, as if it were the answer he'd hoped for, and turns back to Bram.

"Coll Brannock. I keep accounts for Gerrit Thale, down past the Juggler. You'll have had his name from Vell, and nothing kind with it." He keeps his hands loose at his sides and nowhere near his coat. "So, plain. Thale will buy that box off you as it sits, lock shut and wax on. Sixty gold, counted out on that block there, and you never have to walk it back up the street. Whatever Vell's promised you, you'd get it on his counter, on his terms, when he feels like it." He lets that settle, then adds one thing more, in the same even voice. "I'd only want to know first whether anybody's had the lid up. A box with the wax on is worth something. A box without it is firewood."

Out at the gate the young smith shifts his weight against the post. Tobin doesn't lift the mallet. The dog's growl runs on under everything, steady as a kettle, and at the end of the gallery the light from Sefa's beads lies gold across the dead man's threshold.

Tobin has set his mallet on the barrel rim and stands with both hands on it, watching the gate. Nobody is striking anything, so the hammer-count you meant to keep has nothing to count. He nods slightly, as if that were the answer he'd hoped for, and turns back to Bram.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't look at the gate yet. His hands move first.

He flips the oilcloth back over the die with the dagger's point and folds it closed the way it came, three turns, and only then picks the whole bundle up — through the cloth, never the lead — and pushes it deep into the inside of his jerkin, under the armour, where no purse-cutter's fingers go. The board goes back into its gap, nails pressed home with the heel of his hand, and he drags his boot once through the dust at the ends so the smudges are gone. Ten heartbeats, no more.

"Mallet's stopped and the dog's on its chain toward the gate," he says, quiet and flat, already up. "That's not the pie-seller. Sefa — the box is yours. Pick it up, hold it against you, seal side in, and stand where Bram is. Bram — don't go down the stair. Whoever it is can talk up to us the way we talked up to Wenna. Stairs favour the man on top."

He slips past them to the open doorway and takes the hinge side of the frame, a shoulder's width back from the light, where he can see the gate and the stretch of Coast Way beyond it without being a face in a window. Shortbow's still in the pack; it's the dagger that stays in his hand, low along his thigh.

"And for what it's worth," he adds, barely moving his lips, "that die drank the light. The grooves came up brighter after the rest. Lead doesn't do that. Whatever Ferr was sealing with, it wasn't rent receipts."

scenes.narration:
Pell folds the oilcloth back over the die with the point of the dagger, three stiff turns, the way it came. It closes into its old shape as if it had never been opened. Then he picks the whole bundle up through the cloth, without touching the lead, and pushes it deep inside his jerkin under the armour. It sits there heavy, a cold weight against his ribs that doesn't warm. The board goes back into its gap. The loose nails drop into their loose holes, and he presses them home with the heel of his hand. One drag of his boot through the dust at the board's ends and the thumb-and-finger smudges are gone, leaving only a scuff, the kind a broom misses in any corner. The whole thing takes about ten heartbeats.

He says what he has to say quietly, already standing. It goes no further than the room and the gallery.

He crosses to the doorway, takes the hinge side of the frame and stands a shoulder's width back from the light, with the dagger held low along his thigh. From there the yard lies open below him: the pale stave stacks, the chopping block, the shed roof with its unbroken moss. Tobin stands at his barrel with both hands on the mallet and isn't using it. The brown dog has stretched its chain taut toward the cart gate and is growling low and steady.

The young smith with the burn-scarred arms is back at the gate. He leans on the post with his arms folded and looks into the yard.

Thirty-odd feet inside the gate, on the packed earth, stands a lean man in a good brown coat. He's bareheaded, with his hands loose at his sides and well away from the coat. He has stopped short of the stair. From the end of the gallery Pell can't see who he's facing. The foot of the stair is under the lip of the gallery boards, out of his line, and the man is talking up and under it to someone Pell can't see. His voice carries clearly in the quiet yard. It's the Gate, round in the vowels and flat at the ends: *Coll Brannock. I keep accounts for Gerrit Thale.* Then he gets to business: sixty gold for the box as it sits, lock shut and wax on, counted out on the chopping block. *I'd only want to know first whether anybody's had the lid up. A box with the wax on is worth something. A box without it is firewood.*

Wenna's voice came down from the rail a moment before, flat as a board. *It's paid for. Talk to them.*

While he talks, Brannock's eyes go up the gallery to the end door, where the gold light spills out over the threshold. They rest on the bright square of the doorway, on the light itself, and slide off it again. In that glare the shadow beside the hinge is just a shadow. His look comes back down to whoever stands at the foot of the stair, and he waits, the way a man waits with a figure on the table.

Inside the room the board lies flush. The pen still lies square to the edge of the table, and the box sits under its green seal. The dog keeps growling.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps out of the room onto the gallery, drawing the door back toward the frame behind her, though not enough to latch it — enough that a man below can't see straight past her to the table. She crosses to the rail a few feet from Wenna and lays her hands one over the other on the old wood. The little light from her beads pales in the morning glare but doesn't go out.

"Master Brannock," she says, and her voice carries down as clearly as if she were speaking across a sickroom. "You'd want to know whether anybody's had the lid up." She pauses a beat, then says, "So would I. You were here yesterday afternoon, at the block there, with your purse open. Did you touch the door? Did you come up the stair, even to the middle tread? Did you put your eye to the window?" Her fingers rest easy on the rail. "A man who keeps accounts for Gerrit Thale will know all the marks that move money in this town. Perhaps you already know whose wax is on that seam. And that is the first honest thing I'd want from you before any coin is counted." She lets the word hang, not quite friendly. "Sixty gold's a fine offer for a box you can't see past the lid."

“You’re particular about the wax. Describe the seal you’re expecting, and tell me why Thale wants these papers. If he has a claim to them, I’ll hear it.”

I stay between Brannock and the stair, without closing the distance.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't step into the light. He stays in the shadow of the hinge and lets Brannock go on looking at the glare.

He counts the yard instead. Brannock, hands wide of his coat — a man who wants to be seen unarmed, which means he's counted on someone else being armed. The smith's lad at the gatepost, arms folded, blocking the width of it with his body as if by accident. Tobin, still, not frightened, just a man who's stopped working because his yard has become someone else's business. The dog pulling toward the gate, not the man in the coat. He looks past the lad into the Coast Way for the rest of it — a second man idling at the pie hatch, a cart stopped where no cart need stop, anyone in the street who's facing the yard instead of walking past it.

Then, without turning his head, barely a breath over his shoulder to whichever of the two is still behind him in the room:

"Sixty, sight unseen, from a man who sent a boy to watch us and chalked a ring on the back post. He's not buying ledgers. He wants to know if the lid's been up because he knows what's *not* in that box anymore — and he's hoping it's still in the room. It isn't. It's under my ribs." A beat. "Whoever's at the foot of the stair, let them talk. We don't sell, we don't say no yet, and nobody names Vell's number. If it comes to coin, Bram can tell him Vell's paying more and Thale can bid against Vell to his face. If it comes to the other thing, the lad at the gate is the one who'll move first — he's been told to stop the gate, and he's young enough to do it badly."

He eases the dagger back into its sheath and lets his hand drift to the pack strap instead, where the shortbow is. Not drawn. Just closer.

scenes.narration:
Pell stays in the shadow on the hinge side of the frame. Brannock goes on looking up at the glare and doesn't see the man standing beside it.

Pell counts the yard. Watching a street for the people who aren't walking it is part of his trade, and the Coast Way doesn't make him work hard.

The young smith has come off the gatepost and stands just inside the gate on the left, arms folded, watching his master's back. The gate is wide enough for a cart, and he fills about a third of it. He doesn't move to fill more. His weight is on his heels and his hands are empty. He doesn't look like a man posted to hold a gate. He looks like a boy who walked his master here and is waiting to be told he can go. Tobin stands at his barrel with both hands on the mallet head. He isn't frightened, just still, the way a man goes still when his yard has turned into somebody else's business. The brown dog has gone quiet. Its chain is still taut, and its eyes are on the man in the brown coat.

Beyond the gate there's no stopped cart and nobody loitering at the pie hatch. The bench up the street is still empty. Across the Coast Way, though, is the open door of a smithy whose forge isn't working, and a heavy man in a leather apron leans in it eating an apple. He doesn't look at the apple. He faces the cooper's gate, and he's been chewing the same bite for a while.

Pell's words over his shoulder go into the room behind him, and nobody is there to hear them. There's only the table under the shut window, the box with its green seam, and the pen laid square. The whisper stays in the room with the dead man's things.

Down in the yard Brannock is still talking, and his voice carries the way it did before. Questions come down to him from the gallery and up from the foot of the stair, and he answers them in order like items on a bill. He never set foot on the stair. He expects Vell's seal, a balance over a V in red. Thale wants to know whether it's luck that Vell's road debtors keep losing their wagons. Then he raises the price to seventy, paid on Thale's own table past the Juggler, if all three bearers come and say to Thale's face which room the box came out of and what they saw there. Once, while he waits for an answer, his eyes go back to the end of the gallery, to the gold light coming out of Jassan's door. They stay there a moment longer than they did the first time before they come down again.

Pell sheathes the dagger and lets his hand drift back to the pack strap. Under the flap his fingers find the curve of the horn-backed bow, and its string is still coiled loose beside it. The bow is unstrung, the way he carries it on the road, and stringing it is two hands and a few heartbeats' work. The dagger was the only thing ready.

In the yard Brannock folds his hands in front of his coat and waits. Across the street the man in the smithy doorway takes another bite of his apple.

Pell's words over his shoulder go into the room behind him, and nobody is there to hear them. There's only the table under the shut window, the box with its green seam, and the pen laid square. The whisper stays in the room with the dead man's things.

Down in the yard Brannock is still talking, and his voice carries the way it did before. Questions come down to him from the gallery and up from the foot of the stair, and he answers them in order like items on a bill. He never set foot on the stair. He expects Vell's seal, a balance over a V in red. Thale wants to know whether it's luck that Vell's road debtors keep losing their wagons. Then he raises the price to seventy, paid on Thale's own table past the Juggler, if all three bearers come and say to Thale's face which room the box came out of and what they saw there. Once, while he waits for an answer, his eyes go back to the end of the gallery, to the gold light coming out of Jassan's door. They stay there a moment longer than they did the first time before they come down again.

Pell sheathes the dagger and lets his hand drift back to the pack strap. Under the flap his fingers find the curve of the horn-backed bow, and its string is still coiled loose beside it. The bow is unstrung, the way he carries it on the road, and stringing it is two hands and a few heartbeats' work. The dagger was the only thing ready.

In the yard Brannock folds his hands in front of his coat and waits. Across the street the man in the smithy doorway takes another bite of his apple.

messages.text:
“We haven’t lifted the lid. And a higher offer doesn’t make the box ours to sell.”

At the mention of the missing wagons, my expression hardens. “I’ve guarded that road ten years. If Thale has names and dates behind what you’re saying, I’m willing to hear them. That’s a separate conversation from buying this box.”

I glance toward the young man at the gate, then back to Brannock.

“One more thing. There’s a chalk mark on the back gatepost. Was that your doing, and what’s it meant to tell the next man who comes here?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa tilts her head a little at Brannock's phrasing, setting one knuckle against her lips as if considering a sick man's pulse. Then she lowers her hand and smiles, faintly and without warmth.

"You said *whose wax it is* just now, as if there were such a box and you knew real wax when you saw it." She leans her wrists on the rail, easy and unbuttoned, the beads glinting. "I think you know something's blown in on Vell's luck that isn't only luck, and that the box in that room may hold a man's ledgers but also a great many bad mornings on the road. Your master isn't the only one whose debtors vanish between Beregost and Nashkel. He's only the one prepared to pay to learn why."

She gives the yard a slow, unhurried look, the same look she had in Vell's counting-house when she saw him flinch toward a dead clerk's clean desk. "We'll carry the box down," she says, "and we'll carry it where we've been engaged to carry it. But I'll make you a better offer than a purse on the block, Master Brannock: answer me true here, before Tobin's mallet starts again, and I'll tell you what we've seen in this room — enough for a careful man to decide whether Thale's price is too high."

She lifts one hand and counts off on her fingers, the old hospice habit, each point as level as a prayer. "One: who told Thale the strongbox was in the room, and when? Two: does Gerrit Thale know a man who signs with green wax and an eye shut under a pair of scales? Three: did Thale himself put word along the road, or only wait by his own lamp, as he does now?" She curls her fingers down and closes the list. "And four, least but not last: the young man at the gate. Is he yours by hire, or by fear? He marked himself in chalk before ever he followed us. So which of your company drew that ring, and what does it warn against?"

She straightens from the rail and lets the question fall. "Answer me true, and while we talk, your purse stays shut. Lie to me once and I'll know, and so will you, and the cabal will have its box but not its witness."

Behind her, the door to the dead man's room stands half-open, the white-gold light within like a candle no draft reaches. The morning hammering has stopped. In the quiet, the dog whines once, as if at something passing the gate.

scenes.narration:
Coll Brannock hears Bram out without moving. When Bram mentions the road, his eyes rest on Bram's face a little longer, the way a man rechecks a sum when one line comes out different from what he expected.

"Not lifted. Then it's worth what I said." He leaves it there. "And you've guarded that road. That I didn't know."

He takes the chalk first, since it was asked first.

"The ring's mine. I had the lad draw it." He doesn't look round at the gate. "Jory. Hired by the day, two silver, and glad of it. He's no fighter. Back in the Gate that mark tells the next crew this house is spoken for, so keep your hands off. Down here nobody reads it. I had it put there out of habit, and in case somebody up from the Gate came by who could." He stops for a moment. "It looks as if somebody did."

Then he turns his face up to the rail and Sefa, and takes her four in order, like lines on a bill.

"Who told Thale the box was in the room. Nobody. He's watched Jassan Ferr carry that box home up the Coast Way of an evening, under his arm, more than once this summer. A clerk who takes his master's books home is a clerk with something on his mind. When the temple's handcart came down this street three days ago, Mister Thale knew whose it was by noon. Lenders hear about deaths early. A dead man's debts don't wait."

"Green wax, scales over a shut eye." He shakes his head once. "No. It's not a mark I know, and I've seen most of the marks that move money between here and the Gate. I'll tell him you asked, though. He'll want to know." He doesn't say what Thale might make of it.

"Did he put word along the road." A small dry movement at the corner of his mouth. "He sits by his lamp, mistress, as you say. And he listens at the Juggler, where the caravan men drink when they've got nothing left to drive." He looks back to Bram. "Since you asked for names, here's one for nothing. Harl Dobbin. He borrowed off Vell in the spring. In high summer he lost his wagons and four guards past the Lionsfang ford, and nobody came back to say how. A month before that, Vell sold his note on. Dobbin will tell you who bought it, if you stand him a drink. He drinks on Mister Thale's credit now." He lets that settle. "The rest of the names Thale keeps in a book, with the dates. At his table, not in this yard."

"Hire or fear. Hire. I told you, two silver."

Sefa's last word is still in the air of the yard, and it seems to amuse him a little. "Cabal. That's a big word for two lenders and a dead clerk." The amusement goes as quickly as it came. "You'll have noticed I haven't opened my purse."

He unfolds his hands.

"That's your four, and every one of them true. You can test them on whoever you like. You owe me your half: what's in that room, what you saw. I'll take it at Mister Thale's table, from all three of you, any hour before dark. The seventy stands till then. After dark Vell has his box, or he doesn't, and it stops being my business." He nods up to the rail. "Mistress Pike."

"Master Brannock," Wenna says. She stays at the rail with both hands on the wood and says nothing more.

He turns and walks back across the packed earth at the same unhurried pace he came in at. At the gate Jory falls in a half-step behind him, and the two of them go out onto the Coast Way and turn south. In the doorway of the cold smithy across the street, a heavy man in a leather apron throws an apple core into the gutter and goes inside.

Tobin watches the gate a moment longer. Then he takes the mallet off the barrel's rim and brings it down on the hoop, thock, and goes on, thock, as if the yard were his own again. Under the shed's eave the brown dog turns round once on its sack, lies down with its chin toward the stair, and doesn't take its eyes off the end of the gallery. Behind Sefa the light of her beads still lies gold across the dead man's threshold, through the gap in the half-shut door.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell swears once, silently, at an empty room — he's been briefing a dead man's table.

He fixes that first. Two steps back into the room, the bow comes out of the pack, foot braced on the lower limb, string looped over the nock with the ease of a man who's done it in the dark. It takes the heartbeats it takes. Then he slings it on his shoulder, loose, and pulls the arrows round to where his hand finds them without looking.

The box he takes next — because nobody else has, and the job is the job. He lifts it off the table with the oilcloth from the dead man's nightstand wrapped round his hands rather than his skin, turns it seal-side against his chest, and feels the weight of it: paper-heavy, as Vell said, or lighter than paper should be. He notes which.

Then back to the hinge side of the door, still in the shadow, and he lets the yard play out another few breaths. The lad at the gate is nobody's wall. The man to mind is across the street with the apple, who's chewed one bite long enough to grow a beard on it. Pell marks where he'd have to stand to put an arrow in that doorway, and where the gallery rail would give him cover from it, and leaves it at that.

Only when Brannock's eyes come up the gallery a third time does Pell step out — not far, a half-pace, so the gold light falls across the iron-bound box in his arms and the green wax under his forearm. He gives the man in the brown coat a civil nod, the way one hired hand nods to another across a yard.

"It's all right, Master Brannock," he calls down, easy, "the lid's not been up. You can tell your master that, and save him seventy." He hefts the box an inch. "This goes where it was hired to go. If Master Thale wants to bid, Vell keeps a counter at the other end of the street, and it's open all day."

And he stays there by the rail, box held close, bow on his shoulder, one eye on the open smithy door across the Coast Way — letting Bram and Sefa do whatever they were going to do with the fact that the third bearer is now visibly carrying the thing, and visibly not coming down to the chopping block.

scenes.narration:
Pell takes two steps back into the room, out of the light. He brings the bow out of the pack, sets his foot on the lower limb, bends it and slips the string over the nock in one practised pull. He's done it often enough in the dark. It takes the heartbeats it takes, and then the horn-backed bow is strung and slung loose on his shoulder. He works the quiver round on his hip until his hand finds the arrows without looking.

Then the box. His hand goes to the nightstand for the oilcloth and finds no cloth there. There's only the dark vial and its stopper lying on its side, and the bitter smell rising off the stained boards below. The only oilcloth in the room is the one folded three times round the lead die, cold against his ribs under his jerkin. The strongbox stays where Jassan left it, on the table under the shut window, its green seam whole.

All the while the yard talks, and in that quiet every word comes up to him. Brannock goes through his answers like lines on a bill. The chalk ring is his. Jory drew it for two silver a day, and *down here nobody reads it. It looks as if somebody did.* Thale watched Jassan carry the box home of an evening all summer. Then a name given away for nothing: Harl Dobbin, a borrower of Vell's, who lost his wagons and four guards past the Lionsfang ford a month after Vell sold his note on. The seventy stands till dark, at Thale's table, with all three bearers and an account of the room. Somewhere in there Brannock nods up to the rail and says *Mistress Pike*, but Pell is at the nightstand with his back to the door when he says it.

When he gets back to the hinge side of the frame, Brannock already has his back to the gallery. He crosses the packed earth at the same unhurried pace he came in at and doesn't look up again. At the gate Jory falls in half a step behind him, and the two of them turn south down the Coast Way.

Across the street the heavy man in the leather apron throws his apple core into the gutter and goes into the cold smithy. The doorway stays open and dark behind him. Pell marks it anyway. Anyone standing a pace back inside that door would have a clear line straight up to Jassan's threshold. The gallery rail would cover a man standing low beside the end door, and nothing would cover him in the doorway itself.

Down in the yard, Tobin lifts the mallet off the barrel rim and brings it down on the hoop. Thock. Thock. The brown dog turns once on its sack and lies down with its chin toward the stair and its eyes on the end of the gallery. Behind Pell the room holds what it held before: the table, the pen laid square, and the iron-bound box under its green wax. He stands in the doorway with the bow strung on his shoulder.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays at the rail until Brannock and Jory are past the gate and gone south, then lets her breath out slowly, the kind of sigh that holds more listening than relief. Her hands remain loose on the wood. When she speaks, it is quiet enough for Bram below and Wenna beside her, not for the street.

"Every one of those four was true. I think he meant them to be." She watches the last of the morning dust settle where the two men passed. "But he gave us the one thing he didn't set out to give. That chalk circle wasn't to keep us off. It was to keep some other crew off — Gate, he said, as if that mattered. He was more surprised that it was read than that this room holds a box worth a man's own ledgers. He didn't expect company that could read the wall." A pause. "And he's not afraid of us. He's afraid of what's in the room. He asked after the lid like a man asking if the dead have sat up."

Then she turns a little toward Wenna, her voice gentling into the pitch she'd use at a patient's bedside. "You hear everything in this yard, you said. My friend Pell — did you hear him go? Which way, and when? It isn't like him to leave the gate before he's seen the room." She doesn't make it an accusation; she says *my friend* the way one says the name of someone not yet lost.

And down to Bram: "If she can't say, a slow circuit of the lane and the back gate. Quietly. He won't have gone far. If he has, come back and we'll shape this another way."

She straightens, one hand still on the rail, the other reaching back until her fingertips rest against the edge of the half-shut door, not pushing it open, only keeping the dark and the gold light in their places. "I said we'd take Thale's table before dark, and I'll keep that. But not one of us goes there without the other two."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I wait until Brannock and Jory are out of earshot, then speak quietly to Sefa.

“Odda’s letter says Harl died. Brannock says Harl Dobbin’s alive and drinking at the Juggler. Could be different men. We need to ask, not guess. And that burned letter’s talk of notes sold before wagons went missing fits his story closely enough to trouble me.”

I look toward Ferr’s door. “Before we move the box, tell me what you found on that seal. Is it safe to carry without touching the wax?”

Then I call across the yard, loud enough to reach behind the stave shed: “Pell! Brannock’s gone. We need a word.”

I listen for an answer.

scenes.narration:
Brannock and Jory are past the gate and out of sight to the south, and the yard is down to the people who live in it. Sefa lets her breath go at the rail and says what she has to say quietly, for Bram below and the woman beside her. Wenna listens with both hands on the wood. When Sefa turns the gentler voice on her and asks after *my friend Pell*, the landlady gives her a long sideways look.

"Mind, he never went anywhere." She tips her head at the half-shut door behind Sefa's hand. "He came up my stair while you two were stood at that sill. Came up on the nail ends, too. I barely heard him, and I hear that stair in my sleep. He asked me about the dog, polite as a curate, and went in along the wall. He hasn't come out past me." She looks at the end shutter, its hook still webbed into its eye. "Not that way either."

Down at the foot of the stair, Bram keeps his voice low for Sefa. In this yard that isn't low enough. The names reach the rail as plainly as anything Tobin's barrels hear, and Wenna's head turns before he has finished.

"Harl." She says it flatly, the way she named the rent. "If it's a dead Harl you want, that's Harl Brand. Carter. Drove for whoever'd hire him on the Nashkel run, and his chest gave out on him in the spring. Dobbin's another man. Dobbin's alive and drinking, more's the pity for whoever he owes." She lets the keys alone. "And if Odda Brand's writing letters to hired men about Vell's box, that's her business and yours. I'll not carry it up the street to him. Nobody pays me to."

She doesn't ask what the letter says.

Bram turns from the rail and lifts his voice across the yard toward the stave shed, loud enough to carry behind it and into the lane. *Pell! Brannock's gone. We need a word.*

The call goes out over the packed earth, the chopping block and the pale staves. Nothing comes back from behind the shed. The stacks stand as empty as they were when Bram last looked, and the lane behind the fence is quiet. Tobin glances up at the shout, decides it's no concern of his, and brings the mallet down. Thock. The brown dog lifts its head off its paws and looks at Bram, then past him, up to the end of the gallery, where Sefa's fingertips rest on the edge of the dead man's door. Gold light still leaks through the gap along the frame. Out on the Coast Way, a cart goes by toward the smithies, and the sun has climbed high enough to put the whole gallery in light.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell looks at the vial on its side, the stain under it, and gives up on the oilcloth. He picks the box up bare-handed, by the iron bands, and holds it against his chest with the seam turned in. He weighs it as he lifts — paper-heavy, or lighter than Vell led them to expect — and keeps the answer to himself for now.

He steps out onto the gallery, low along the rail as he goes, and stops where the boards and the end post put wood between him and that dark smithy door across the street.

"Mistress Pike," he says, civil, not loud. "The smith across the way with the cold forge and the apple — whose shop is that? And is it usual for him to have no fire lit at this hour?"

Then down the stair to the other two, keeping the box between his body and the yard. He doesn't stop at the bottom; he draws them into the lee of the stave stacks, out of the gate's line.

"We go now, while Brannock's walking south and before anyone thinks better of letting us." Low, quick. "Three things before we're in the street. One — the wax on this seam is green. Vell told us red, scales and a V. The seal that's *whole* isn't his, and he'll see that the moment we set it on his counter. So we decide now what we say when he does, not then. Two — what pressed that green wax is under my jerkin. Lead, scales over a closed eye, foreign letters round the rim, and a notch on the handle made to fit something else. Ferr kept it under his floor and walked the boards over it till his heart gave out. Three — Brannock gave us a name for free: Harl Dobbin, lost four guards at the Lionsfang ford a month after Vell sold his note on. That's Odda's Harl, Bram, or I'm a patriar."

He shifts the box. "I'll carry it. Bram, walk on my street side; Sefa, behind us where you can see back. We go up the Coast Way the way we came, on the far side from that smithy, and we don't cross in front of its door. If anyone wants it between here and Vell's, they'll have to want it in daylight with the whole street watching."

scenes.narration:
The vial lies where it has lain for three days, and Pell gives up on finding a cloth. He takes the box bare-handed by its iron bands. The oak is cold, and the bands are rough with old rust under his fingers. The box comes off the table heavier than its size suggests, a solid, dead weight like bound paper packed tight. When he tips it to bring the seam round to his chest, something inside shifts. It isn't a rattle. It's a short, flat slide, as if a book or a sheaf had a finger's width of room and used it, and then it settles. He holds it in against him with the green seam turned to his chest.

The wax meets him at exactly the wrong spot. Under his jerkin, right where he holds the box, the oilcloth bundle presses hard against his ribs. With the box held close, the edge of the lid seam sits on that lump, and he can feel the hard curve of the lead through two layers of cloth. That seal is three days old and has never been warm since.

He steps out onto the gallery and keeps low along the rail. He stops where the end post and the rail boards put solid wood between him and the street. From there the cold smithy across the Coast Way is just a dark doorway. A pace or two inside it, a broad shape sits on something low, an anvil block or a keg, facing out. It doesn't move. A man resting, or a man waiting, and from here the two look the same.

Wenna hears him ask and answers without leaving the rail.

"Osric Hask's. He's gone down to Nashkel after ore, a fortnight back, and there's been no fire in that forge since. He leaves Dunn to mind the door." Her mouth goes thin. "Dunn minds it sitting down. Usual for Dunn. Not usual for Hask."

The stair complains under him on the way down. Carrying the box he can't keep to the nail ends, and every tread gets its say. At the bottom he doesn't stop. He goes straight into the lee of the stave stacks, where the pale bundles block the gate's line. There, low and quick, he says his three things and how they'll walk, with the box held against his chest and the seam turned in.

The yard is quiet enough that the gallery hears it. When he gets to Harl Dobbin and *that's Odda's Harl*, Wenna's voice comes down over the rail, flat as a plank.

"Brand. Harl Brand, the carter, his chest gave out in the spring. Dobbin's another man, alive and drinking. I've said it once already this morning." She doesn't say it louder than she needs to. She doesn't say it softer either.

Tobin's mallet comes down on the hoop. Thock. Under the shed's eave the brown dog has stood up. It isn't pulling toward the gate now. It's watching the box against Pell's chest, its ears forward, the way it watched Jassan's door. Out past the cart gate the Coast Way runs bright and busy toward Vell's end of town. Across the street the smithy door stays open and dark, and the shape inside it hasn't moved.

opening.narration:
Beregost wakes to hammers. From every smithy along the street the ringing comes through the shutters of Ostrin Vell's counting-house, where the morning light falls on brass scales and rows of bound ledgers. Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway stand at the long counter. The three of you met here only this morning, and Vell has just hired you together.

Vell lays the terms out a second time, tapping the counter with one finger at each point. Jassan Ferr, his clerk, died three days ago in a rented room above the cooper's yard on the Coast Way. In that room is a locked strongbox of ledgers. Vell wants it here before nightfall today, unopened, with its seal whole. On delivery he will pay seventy-five gold for the three of you to share. Not a copper before.

Beside the counter stands a clerk's desk. Its stool is pushed neatly under it, the inkwell is capped and the blotter is clean, as if someone had tidied it and no one had sat there since. Vell does not look at it. He looks from Sefa to Pell to Bram, folds his hands on the counter and waits. "The Coast Way is not far, and the day will not wait for you. Is there anything you need to ask me before you go?"

Where you are: Ostrin Vell's counting-house, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa presses her palms together over the beads on her wrist and asks Vell how Ferr died, saying she'd like to know if it was fever before anyone opens his door. She asks whether anyone else holds a key to the room or has a claim on his things, a landlord or kinsman. She also asks whether the seal on the box is Vell's mark or Ferr's. Pell, who has been resting against the end of the counter, straightens and counts his questions off on his fingers. He asks who holds the key and whether they know you're coming or might send for the Fist. He asks about the box's size, weight, lock and seal, so he knows what "whole" looks like. He asks whether anyone has been in the room since the death, and whether anyone else has asked about the ledgers. He finishes by asking whether anyone in Beregost would rather the box stayed where it is. He keeps his voice easy, and his eyes are on Vell's hands.

Vell hears you all out without interrupting. He lifts one finger and answers in the order the questions came.

"His heart. The landlady found him in the morning, in his chair. No fever. The room is not unpleasant." He pauses. "It was not unpleasant when I last stood in it, at least. That was a month ago."

A second finger. "The key is with the landlady. Wenna Pike. She owns the rooms over the cooper's yard. Tobin the cooper has the yard and the shop below. Jassan had no kin in Beregost. His mother is dead, years ago, in the Gate. The temple took his body for burial. Since then, Wenna and whoever she lets in. I have not been."

He turns to Pell. "The box. Oak, bound in iron. This long." His hands set themselves on the counter about a foot and a half apart. "One man carries it. Heavy with paper, nothing else. A brass lock. The key is here, with me." He doesn't say where, and his hands don't move toward any drawer. "The seal is mine. Red wax across the lid seam, my mark. Scales, with a V beneath."

To you he gives a short nod and pulls a sheet of paper from under the counter. He writes quickly and plainly, in a moneylender's hand: *Wenna Pike: the bearers collect Jassan Ferr's strongbox on my behalf. O. Vell.* He warms a stick of red wax over the lamp, lets a drop fall at the foot of the page and presses a brass ring into it. When he lifts the ring the mark is just as he said: a small balance with a V beneath it, sharp in the red. He blows on it once and slides the note across to you.

Then he gets to Pell's last question, and to who else has asked.

"Has anyone asked." Vell squares the ink pot with the edge of the counter. "No one has come here asking for Jassan's ledgers." His hands are flat and still on the wood.

"Who would rather it stayed put." He thinks about it honestly, or seems to. "Gerrit Thale keeps a counting-room at the south end of town, past the Jovial Juggler. He would like anything that is mine. He is a lender, not a cutpurse. Walk. You need not go quiet for Thale." He shuts the ledger in front of him. "Wenna Pike will want something from you. She always wants something. Jassan's debts were Jassan's."

He doesn't offer to pay them, and he doesn't look at the clerk's desk. Outside, on the Coast Way, a cart rattles past toward the smithies, and the hammers go on ringing through the shutters.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Vell's Note of Authority

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Vell's strongbox
+ Quest: Vell's strongbox

Where you are: Vell's counting-room, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You let the wax cool, fold the note clear of the seal and stow it. You tell Vell that if Wenna wants rent before she releases the box, you'll bring him her demand, since you agreed to carry a box and not to settle Ferr's debts. Then you turn to Sefa and Pell, ask if they're ready, and head for the cooper's yard with your sword sheathed.

Before that, Pell had pushed off the counter and asked Vell what Wenna Pike would want, how far behind Ferr was, and whether the note buys only the box or the room's contents too. He glanced at the clerk's desk and told you to keep the note dry. Then he said he wanted to see the yard before knocking: front, back, and under Ferr's window. He moved toward the door.

Vell answered Pell first. Wenna will want rent. Ferr was behind, but Vell doesn't know by how much; a room over Tobin's yard is cheap, and Jassan didn't spend much. Ten days ago Ferr asked for his wage early and Vell refused, and Wenna may or may not know. The note covers the box, he says, and the ledgers in it are his. The bed, the coat and the debts are not his and he doesn't want them. If she claims she's owed, she's owed by Ferr, and she can settle with the temple, which has the body.

When you put the note away, Vell nodded shortly and told you to bring Wenna's number, and he'd decide then.

Sefa pressed her palms to the counter, her beads clicking once, and asked quietly what you should do if the box had already been opened, with the seal broken or the lid forced. Vell hesitated. Then he said to bring it as found, to him and to nobody else, with no stops on the way. If you learn who opened it, bring him the name. The terms don't change: unopened, seal whole, before nightfall. Anything else is not what he hired you for. He looked down at his ledger, and the room was quiet apart from the hammers.

Pell has the door open. Outside, the Coast Way is busy: a smith's boy hauling a bucket of slack-water, a carter leaning on his reins, coal smoke low over the cobbles. You follow him onto the step with the note dry under your arm. A few hundred feet down on the same side stands the cooper's yard: pale stacks of barrel staves against a board fence, a cart-wide gate, and above the shop a row of shuttered windows under the eaves. One shutter is closed and the rest are open. Behind you, through the open door, Sefa is still at the counter and Vell has not lifted his eyes from the ledger.

Where you are: Vell's counting-house step, Coast Way · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa spoke from the doorway, telling Vell that if someone other than your party came for the thing before nightfall, he should send no one to warn them, as they would manage whatever was in the street. Vell did not look up. His pen stopped over the ledger.

"I wasn't going to send anyone," he says. Then the pen moves again, and that is all she gets from him.

Out on the step the morning is bright and loud. You stand to one side of the door with your shield rim against your boot and watch the street the way you used to watch a road before the wagons came up. You don't look for trouble. You look for whoever isn't busy.

Sefa comes out through the door, blinking in the glare, and falls in with you and Pell on the Coast Way. Pell has already stepped down into the street and gone across to the far side, where he can look over a row of windows without standing beneath them. He told you quietly to walk with him or wait for her, but not to go in until all three of you are at the gate. He said the one closed shutter among the open ones might well be the dead man's, and he wants to know who closed it. He then went on down that side at an idle pace, looking over the building and the board fence.

Sefa speaks low, for you and Pell only. She doesn't think Vell lied, but he left something out: he said no one had come asking, not that no one wanted it. She wants to see the street before knocking at Tobin's yard, and she wants a look at that closed shutter.

[Onward] [Request an allowed reroll — Perception: watching the Coast Way for anyone taking an interest in the yard, or in the three of you]

You step aside from the doorway and wait for Sefa. Pell, quietly, you tell to have his look: you will speak to Wenna once Sefa joins you, and if the seal is already broken, the price gets settled before anything is carried back. You don't fancy doing the job and then arguing over whether it counted. From the step you look over the yard's gate and the upper windows, watching for anyone taking an interest in you.

Sefa, before she came out, told Vell she would bring the thing as they found it, to him and only him, with no stops. She said that if they learned a name he would have it, though he might not like it. She also told him not to send anyone to warn them if someone else came for it before nightfall. She then came out into the glare and fell in beside you on the Coast Way.

She speaks low, for you and Pell only, though Pell is already across the way and out of earshot, so her question reaches you and the street noise takes the rest. Tobin's mallet goes steadily somewhere in the yard, thock and thock, iron hoops going onto oak.

Your watch pays off in full. Out of the whole busy morning, you pick out the one man who has no business on the Coast Way. He is young and broad in the shoulder, with a smith's forearms speckled with old burn scars, sitting on a bench outside a pie-seller's hatch two doors up on your side. The mug beside him has long since stopped steaming and he hasn't touched it. When the counting-house door opened his head came up, and when Pell crossed the street it turned with him all the way over. Then his eyes went to the cooper's gate and stayed there. He has white on three fingertips of his right hand, chalk or flour, and a pale streak down his trouser leg where he wiped it. A pie-seller's boy would have flour to the elbow. He isn't eating either.

You have his face, his build and the streak fixed in your mind, and you managed it without once looking straight at him. He hasn't noticed he's been marked. It's the old road feeling, the moment before the wagons crest a rise, when you already know where the trouble is sitting.

Back on the bench, the young man picks up his cold mug at last, doesn't drink, and puts it down again. His eyes stay on the cooper's gate.

(While the others were looking elsewhere, a boy pressed a sealed letter into your hand and was gone before anyone else saw. It is for you alone. You break the seal and read:)

«Bram — Harl died owing Ostrin Vell forty gold, and Vell's note for it is in his dead clerk's strongbox — the one Vell has hired you to bring him. Jassan wrote to me before he died: once the box is back, Vell calls the note and takes the house. If that one page were gone before Vell opened the box, there would be nothing to call. Please. I have no one else to ask. — Odda Brand»

Where you are: on the Coast Way outside the counting-house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You fold Odda's letter into your coat, jaw tight for a moment. Quietly, without looking toward the bench, you pass Sefa a warning about the young man outside the pie hatch, and you walk with her toward the gate, keeping him at the edge of your sight. From the street the closed shutter looks no different from the others: weathered boards, a finger's-width gap at the bottom where the frame has warped, and only dark behind it. "Why Thale wants the papers. Mister Thale lends on the same road Vell does, Beregost to Nashkel, caravan men mostly. This past year Vell's paper has had a way of going bad all at once. A man borrows off Vell, and a month or two after, his wagons don't come into Nashkel, and nobody comes in to say why. Thale's lost a debtor or two on that road himself, but nothing like Vell's luck. He'd like to know whether it is luck. That's my master's business, and I've said more of it than he'd thank me for."

"A claim?" He shakes his head once. "None. If Mister Thale had a claim he'd have sent the Fist with a paper, not me with a purse. What he has is an offer." His eyes go from you to Sefa and back. "Carry it to a man who pays on delivery, if the wax suits him, when he's in the mood. Or carry it a bit further south." He moves one loose hand down the Coast Way. "Seventy. Not on the block. On Thale's own table, past the Juggler, and the three of you come with it and tell him to his face which room you lifted it out of and what you saw there. He'll want to hear it from Vell's own bearers. It's worth the ten to him."

He doesn't step closer to the stair. He hasn't moved since he stopped. Neither you nor Sefa has answered his question about the lid, and from the way he folds his hands before his coat, he has noticed and filed it.

At the gate the young smith shifts off the post and stands straight, watching his master's back. Tobin hasn't picked up his mallet. Under the shed's eave the brown dog has stopped growling, but its chain is still taut and its eyes are on the stranger. The sun lies along the gallery boards, and behind Sefa the gold light comes out through the gap in the dead man's door.

Where you are: in the yard between Brannock and the stair · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 14 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa, leaning on the rail beside you, answers Brannock's talk of whose wax it is with a thin, cold smile. She says he seems to know that something has come in on Vell's luck that is not only luck, and that the box may hold a dead man's ledgers along with a good many grim mornings on that road. She says Brannock's master is not alone in having debtors who disappear between Beregost and Nashkel, only the one willing to pay to learn why. The box will be carried down, she says, to where you were engaged to carry it. If he answers her honestly before the mallet starts again, she will tell him what you saw in the room, enough for a careful man to judge whether Thale's price is too high. She puts four questions to him. Who was it that told Thale the strongbox sat in that room, and at what time? Is Thale acquainted with a man who seals with green wax and a shut eye under scales? Did Thale put word along the road himself, or only wait by his lamp? And is the young man at the gate Brannock's by hire or by fear, and who drew the chalk ring? If he lies, she says, she will know.

Brannock hears you out without moving. When you mention the road, his eyes rest on your face a little longer, like a man rechecking a sum. "Not lifted. Then it's worth what I said. And you've guarded that road. That I didn't know."

He takes the chalk first. The ring is his; he had the lad draw it. The lad is Jory, hired by the day for two silver, no fighter. In the Gate the mark tells the next crew a house is spoken for. Down here nobody reads it, and he had it put there from habit, in case someone up from the Gate came by who could. "It looks as if somebody did."

Then he takes Sefa's four in order. Nobody told Thale the box was in the room. Thale watched Jassan Ferr carry it home up the Coast Way of an evening, more than once this summer, and when the temple's handcart came down this street three days ago he knew whose it was by noon. "Lenders hear about deaths early." Green wax and scales over a shut eye: he does not know the mark, and he has seen most of those that move money between here and the Gate. He will tell Thale you asked. Thale sits by his lamp, and he listens at the Juggler, where caravan men drink when they have nothing left to drive.

He looks back to you. "Since you asked for names, here's one for nothing. Harl Dobbin. He borrowed off Vell in the spring. In high summer he lost his wagons and four guards past the Lionsfang ford, and nobody came back to say how. A month before that, Vell sold his note on. Dobbin will tell you who bought it, if you stand him a drink. He drinks on Mister Thale's credit now. The rest of the names Thale keeps in a book, with the dates, at his table, not in this yard." Jory is his by hire, he says, two silver.

Sefa's word "cabal" seems to amuse him. "That's a big word for two lenders and a dead clerk." He notes his purse is still shut. He says every answer was true and you can test them on anyone. You owe him your half: what is in that room and what you saw, at Thale's table, all three of you, any hour before dark. The seventy stands till then. After dark Vell has his box, or he doesn't, and it stops being his business. He nods up to the rail. "Mistress Pike."

"Master Brannock," Wenna says. She stays at the rail, both hands on the wood, and says nothing more.

Brannock walks back across the packed earth at the pace he came in, Jory a half-step behind him, and they go out onto the Coast Way and turn south. In the doorway of the cold smithy across the street, a heavy man in a leather apron throws an apple core into the gutter and goes inside.

Tobin watches the gate a moment, then brings the mallet down on the hoop again, thock, and goes on as if the yard were his own. Under the shed's eave the brown dog turns round once on its sack, lies down with its chin toward the stair, and keeps its eyes on the end of the gallery.

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Sefa's half of the bargain with Coll

Where you are: gallery rail above the yard, outside the dead man's room · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 15 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You wait until Brannock and Jory are out of earshot, then speak quietly to Sefa. You point out that Odda's letter says Harl died, while Brannock says Harl Dobbin is alive and drinking at the Juggler, and that these could be different men. You say you need to ask, not guess, and that the burned letter's talk of notes sold before the wagons went missing fits Brannock's story closely enough to trouble you. You look toward Ferr's door and ask Sefa what she found on the seal, and whether the box can be carried without touching the wax.

Above you at the rail, Sefa, in a voice meant for you and Wenna and not the street, says every one of Brannock's four statements was true, and that she thinks he meant them to be. She says he let slip that the chalk circle was meant to keep another crew off, "Gate" he called it, and that it surprised him more that someone had read the wall than that this room holds a box worth more than a man's own ledgers. He isn't afraid of you, she says, but of what is in the room. She asks Wenna, gently, whether she heard her friend go, and which way. To you she says that if Wenna can't say, you should walk a slow, quiet round of the lane and the back gate, and come back if he has gone far. She will keep her word to take Thale's table before dark, she says, but not one of you goes without the other two. One hand stays on the rail and the other rests on the edge of the half-shut door.

Wenna says the man never went anywhere. He came up her stair while you and Sefa stood at that sill, on the nail ends, so quietly she barely heard him. He asked about the dog, polite as a curate, and went in along the wall. He hasn't come out past her, and not through the end shutter either, its hook still webbed into its eye.

Your low voice carried in this yard, and she heard the name Harl. She says flatly that a dead Harl would be Harl Brand, a carter on the Nashkel run whose chest gave out in the spring. Dobbin is another man, alive and drinking. If Odda Brand writes to hired men about Vell's box, that is your business and hers, and Wenna won't carry it up the street to Brannock. She doesn't ask what the letter says.

You call across the yard toward the stave shed that Brannock is gone and Pell is wanted for a word. Nothing answers from behind the shed. The stacks stand as empty as before, and the lane behind the fence is quiet. Tobin glances up, decides it's no concern of his, and brings the mallet down again. The brown dog lifts its head and looks at you, then past you, up to the end of the gallery, where Sefa's fingertips rest on the dead man's door. Gold light still leaks through the gap along the frame. A cart goes by on the Coast Way toward the smithies, and the sun has climbed high enough to put the whole gallery in light.

Where you are: in the yard at the foot of the stair · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.
